changes.note: Locates the self-similar ansatz in Leray. Gives the precise exclusion results without changing the stated class. Locates the open problem in the primary preprint.
changes.adapted_text: Leray \[[70](#cite-ref70), §20, pp. 224–225\] proposed to look for singular solutions of (1.1) among the backward self-similar ones, $u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}\,U(x/\sqrt{T-t})$. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76), Theorem 1, p. 291\] and Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86), Theorems 1–2, p. 31\] proved that there is no such solution other than zero, under natural integrability conditions on the profile $U$. The next candidate is a solution that is invariant under the scaling of the equations for one scaling factor only, possibly after a rotation: a discretely self-similar <!-- source-page: 2 --> solution. Whether a nonzero solution of this kind exists backward in time, with the bound $|u(t,x)|\le C\,(|x|+\sqrt{T-t})^{-1}$, is the subject of \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.1, preprint p. 22\].

changes.note: Locates the four alternatives while retaining the authors’ claim.
changes.adapted_text: In this paper we prove that smooth solutions of (1.1) can blow up in finite time: there exist smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free data on $\mathbb R^3$, and smooth divergence-free data on $\mathbb T^3$, whose solutions are smooth up to a finite time, at which they blow up. In the formulation of the regularity problem by Fefferman \[[53](#cite-ref53), alternatives (A)–(D), pp. 1–2\], this disproves his statements (A) and (B) and hence proves his statements (C) and (D). The proof has two parts. The first is Theorem 1.1: one smooth discretely self-similar solution of the kind above implies this blow-up. Its proof shows that such a solution is stable in $\dot H^1$ up to finitely many directions, whatever the spectrum of its linearization is. The second is Theorem 7.1: such a solution exists near an approximate one that satisfies explicit inequalities, which we call a certificate.

changes.note: Makes explicit how the decay bound brings a stationary profile within Tsai’s theorem and supplies the precise literature locators. Adds the verified primary-source locator. changes.adapted_text: Leray’s self-similar solutions correspond to solutions of the first two equations of (1.2) that are independent of $s$. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76), Theorem 1, p. 291\] exclude nonzero profiles in $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$. Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86), Theorems 1–2, p. 31\] excludes them in $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$, $3<p<\infty$, and under local energy estimates. The bound (1.3) puts every slice of a profile in $L^6$: it is bounded near the origin and its sixth power is integrable at infinity. A profile independent of $s$ would therefore be zero. Thus the nonzero profile required here must depend on $s$. For discretely self-similar solutions, Open Problem 5.1 of \[[13](#cite-ref13), preprint p. 22\] asks whether a backward solution with the Type I bound, rotated or not, remains bounded up to time $T$; iteration of (1.5) multiplies any nonzero velocity magnitude by $\lambda^{-n/2}$ along points approaching $(T,0)$, so a solution that remains bounded is zero, and by Remark 1.2 a smooth solution that is not zero is the field (1.4) of a profile. When $R=I$, Chae and Wolf \[[26](#cite-ref26), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3, preprint pp. 2–3\] proved that the Type I bound holds for every smooth backward discretely self-similar solution that is continuous in time with values in $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$ for some $p\in[3,\infty)$, and that a smooth solution with this bound is zero if its scaling factor $e^{S/2}$ is close enough to $1$: the period $S$ of a profile with $R=I$ is bounded below by a positive number that depends only on $C_W$. Pineau and Vicol \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorems 1.6–1.7, pp. 6–7\] gave a quantitative proof and extended the statement to rotations $R$ by an angle at most $cS$, for a constant $c>0$ that depends only on $C_W$. Nonzero solutions with the Type I bound that are self-similar up to a rotation at a constant angular speed in $s$ would give profiles for every period; the question of their existence goes back to Perelman, as recorded by Bradshaw and Tsai \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.2, preprint p. 22\], and they are excluded for small and for large angular speeds \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorem 1.4, p. 4\]. Forward in time, self-similar and discretely self-similar solutions do exist \[[64](#cite-ref64), [87](#cite-ref87), [12](#cite-ref12), [27](#cite-ref27)\], also up to a rotation \[[13](#cite-ref13)\].
changes.authors_text: The self-similar solutions of Leray are the solutions of the first two equations of (1.2) that do not depend on $s$. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76)\] proved that the only such solution with $W\in L^3(\mathbb R^3)$ is zero, and Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86), Theorems 1 and 2\] proved the same for $W\in L^p(\mathbb R^3)$, $3<p<\infty$, and for the self-similar solutions that satisfy local energy estimates. In particular a profile depends on $s$, since its slices lie in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$. For discretely self-similar solutions, Open Problem 5.1 of \[[13](#cite-ref13)\] asks whether a backward solution with the Type I bound, rotated or not, remains bounded up to time $T$; by its self-similarity, a solution that remains bounded is zero, and by Remark 1.2 a smooth solution that is not zero is the field (1.4) of a profile. When $R=I$, Chae and Wolf \[[26](#cite-ref26), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3\] proved that the Type I bound holds for every smooth backward discretely self-similar solution that is continuous in time with values in $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$ for some $p\in[3,\infty)$, and that a smooth solution with this bound is zero if its scaling factor $e^{S/2}$ is close enough to $1$: the period $S$ of a profile with $R=I$ is bounded below by a positive number that depends only on $C_W$. Pineau and Vicol \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorems 1.6 and 1.7\] gave a quantitative proof and extended the statement to rotations $R$ by an angle at most $cS$, for a constant $c>0$ that depends only on $C_W$. Nonzero solutions with the Type I bound that are self-similar up to a rotation at a constant angular speed in $s$ would give profiles for every period; the question of their existence goes back to Perelman, as recorded by Bradshaw and Tsai \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.2\], and they are excluded for small and for large angular speeds \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorem 1.4\]. Forward in time, self-similar and discretely self-similar solutions do exist \[[64](#cite-ref64), [87](#cite-ref87), [12](#cite-ref12), [27](#cite-ref27)\], also up to a rotation \[[13](#cite-ref13)\].

changes.note: Identifies weak L³ from the pointwise bound, the logarithmic growth of the local L³ integral for an identity-isometry profile, and the strong-L³ regularity criterion. Qualifies the axisymmetric criteria and identifies their cited hypotheses.
changes.adapted_text: The decay (1.3) bounds $u_T^*(t)$ uniformly in spatial weak $L^3$. For $R=I$, [Barker and Prange (Corollary 1.1, p. 720)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-021-04122-x) give $\int_{|y|<r}|W(s,y)|^3\,dy\asymp\log r$ for large $r$, uniformly in $s$. Thus no such slice lies in $L^3$. For Leray–Hopf solutions, Escauriaza, Seregin and Šverák exclude singularities under a uniform-in-time $L^3$ bound \[[52](#cite-ref52), Theorem 1.3, preprint p. 5\]. Several criteria exclude Type I singularities for axisymmetric solutions under additional hypotheses \[[28](#cite-ref28), [29](#cite-ref29), [69](#cite-ref69), [81](#cite-ref81)\]. Chen, Strain, Tsai and Yau assume pressure in $L^{5/3}$ and pointwise velocity bounds on $\mathbb R^3\times(-T_0,0)$ \[[29](#cite-ref29), Theorem 1.1, preprint p. 2\], \[[28](#cite-ref28), Theorem 1.1, preprint p. 2\]. Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin and Šverák add $|u|\le C/r$ for cylindrical radius $r\ge R_0$ \[[69](#cite-ref69), Theorem 6.2, preprint p. 21\]. Seregin and Šverák give a local statement for weak solutions in $L^3$ with pressure in $L^{3/2}$, under a Type I bound on the meridional velocity \[[81](#cite-ref81), Theorem 1.1, preprint p. 4\]. Albritton and Barker \[[1](#cite-ref1)\] proved that a suitable weak solution with a Type I singular point exists if and only if there is a nontrivial mild bounded ancient solution, in the sense of \[[69](#cite-ref69)\], with Type I decay. By \[[1](#cite-ref1), Remark 4.3\], a nontrivial mild ancient solution that is bounded in weak $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$ along a sequence of times, as the field of a profile is, gives a singular weak Leray–Hopf solution of the equations with a force. Theorem 1.1 assumes a discretely self-similar solution and concludes blow-up without force, from smooth, compactly supported data on $\mathbb R^3$ and from smooth data on the torus.
changes.authors_text: By the first bound of (1.3), $u_T^*(t)$ is bounded in weak $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$, uniformly in $t$, and this gives no bound in $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$; for solutions that are bounded in $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$, singularities are excluded by the theorem of Escauriaza, Seregin and Šverák \[[52](#cite-ref52)\]. Singularities of Type I are excluded for axisymmetric solutions \[[28](#cite-ref28), [29](#cite-ref29), [69](#cite-ref69), [81](#cite-ref81)\]. Albritton and Barker \[[1](#cite-ref1)\] proved that a suitable weak solution with a Type I singular point exists if and only if there is a nontrivial mild bounded ancient solution, in the sense of \[[69](#cite-ref69)\], with Type I decay. By \[[1](#cite-ref1), Remark 4.3\], a nontrivial mild ancient solution that is bounded in weak $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$ along a sequence of times, as the field of a profile is, gives a singular weak Leray–Hopf solution of the equations with a force. Theorem 1.1 assumes a discretely self-similar solution and concludes blow-up without force, from smooth, compactly supported data on $\mathbb R^3$ and from smooth data on the torus.

changes.note: Checks both defining conditions of the homogeneous space and separates them from finite kinetic energy. Show why the two decay powers are exactly enough for the working space while the profile can still have infinite kinetic energy.
changes.adapted_text: The field (1.4) of a profile is a smooth solution of (1.1), and we construct the solutions of Theorem 1.1 as perturbations of it. We find the perturbation by a contraction argument for the integral formulation of (1.1), which the field $u_1^*$ satisfies on $[0,1)$ (Proposition 4.1). We work in the space $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ of the divergence-free fields in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ with square integrable gradient, with the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$: at large radius $r$ the volume element contributes $r^2\,dr$. The bounds in (1.3) therefore control $\int |W|^6$ by an integrable $r^{-4}$ tail and $\int|\nabla W|^2$ by an integrable $r^{-2}$ tail, uniformly in $s$. For $\int|W|^2$ the same test gives only a constant times $dr$. On the torus we use the corresponding space of periodic fields of mean zero (Subsections 2.1 and 3.6). By the classical local theory of the equations in $H^1$, a solution of the integral formulation in one of these spaces whose datum is smooth and compactly supported, or smooth on the torus, is a smooth solution (Lemma 2.3).
changes.authors_text: The field (1.4) of a profile is a smooth solution of (1.1), and we construct the solutions of Theorem 1.1 as perturbations of it. We find the perturbation by a contraction argument for the integral formulation of (1.1), which the field $u_1^*$ satisfies on $[0,1)$ (Proposition 4.1). We work in the space $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ of the divergence-free fields in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ with square integrable gradient, with the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$: by (1.3) the gradient of $W(s,\cdot)$ is square integrable, uniformly in $s$, whereas $W(s,\cdot)$ itself need not be. On the torus we use the corresponding space of periodic fields of mean zero (Subsections 2.1 and 3.6). By the classical local theory of the equations in $H^1$, a solution of the integral formulation in one of these spaces whose datum is smooth and compactly supported, or smooth on the torus, is a smooth solution (Lemma 2.3).

changes.note: Names the norm in the convergence statement. Derive the two distinct powers in (1.6) by changing variables in the gradient norm. The paper gives the physical comparison, and the formal support here is the dilation identity.
changes.adapted_text: We write $u^*=u_1^*$. In the self-similar variables with blow-up time $1$, in which $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}\,U(s,y)$, the equations (1.1) are the first two equations of (1.2) for $U$ and a pressure. The profile $W$ is a solution of these that is periodic up to $R$, and we look for solutions $U$ with $U(s)-W(s)\to0$ in $\dot H^1$ as $s\to\infty$. In physical variables the velocity factor and one spatial derivative together contribute $(1-t)^{-1}$, whereas the square root of the volume element contributes $(1-t)^{3/4}$. This accounts for the factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ in (1.6). Thus the rescaled error bound $Ce^{-\kappa s}=C(1-t)^\kappa$ gives the physical gradient error bound $C(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}$.

changes.note: Explains the compact perturbation and the choice of a circle avoiding the spectrum. Locates the cited compact-perturbation argument. Locates the spectral part of the cited construction.
changes.adapted_text: The norm of $\dot H^1$ is subcritical: the scaling $f\mapsto\sqrt\mu\,f(\sqrt\mu\,\cdot)$ of the equations multiplies it by $\mu^{1/4}$. In self-similar variables the linear flow without the terms that come from $W$ is the heat flow up to time $1-e^{-s}$ followed by this scaling with $\mu=e^{-s}$, and therefore its norm on $\dot H^1$ is at most $e^{-s/4}$. The flow linearized about $W$ over one period, followed by the action of $R^{-1}$ on fields, is the monodromy operator $\mathcal M$. The difference from the free flow is compact: Lemma 3.2 gives compactness of the positive-time operators in the integral equation, and the integrable bound (3.7) controls its endpoint (Lemma 4.4). The free-flow norm bounds the essential spectral radius by $e^{-S/4}<1$. Choose $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ with no spectrum on $|z|=\Theta$; outside this circle there are only finitely many eigenvalues, each of finite multiplicity (Lemma 4.5). For a self-similar solution forward in time this is the <!-- source-page: 8 --> argument of Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65), Lemma 2.7, preprint pp. 10–11\]; for a solution that is periodic in self-similar time it is used in \[[17](#cite-ref17), §19, p. 74\], with the same bound for the essential spectral radius.
changes.authors_text: The norm of $\dot H^1$ is subcritical: the scaling $f\mapsto\sqrt\mu\,f(\sqrt\mu\,\cdot)$ of the equations multiplies it by $\mu^{1/4}$. In self-similar variables the linear flow without the terms that come from $W$ is the heat flow up to time $1-e^{-s}$ followed by this scaling with $\mu=e^{-s}$, and therefore its norm on $\dot H^1$ is at most $e^{-s/4}$. The flow linearized about $W$ over one period, followed by the action of $R^{-1}$ on fields, is the monodromy operator $\mathcal M$. It differs from the corresponding free flow by a compact operator. Hence its essential spectral radius is at most $e^{-S/4}<1$, and for a suitable $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ outside the disc of radius $\Theta$ consists of finitely many eigenvalues of finite multiplicity. For a self-similar solution forward in time this is the <!-- source-page: 8 --> argument of Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65), Lemma 2.7\]; for a solution that is periodic in self-similar time it is used in \[[17](#cite-ref17), Section 19\], with the same bound for the essential spectral radius.

changes.note: Describes what the correction acts on while preserving the absence of an unstable-eigenvalue assumption. Expands the two directions of the recurrence and the projection argument that permits compactly supported corrections. Distinguish the rate selected in the proof from ordinary linear instability. No eigenvalue count or preassigned unstable direction is needed. Explain the direction of the two sums and how density of smooth test fields frees the construction from assumptions about the support of the eigenfunctions.

We assume nothing about these eigenvalues. In the program of \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] for non-uniqueness an unstable eigenvalue is the hypothesis, and in \[[17](#cite-ref17)\] the main difficulty is to construct a solution that has one. Only the modes too slow for the desired decay need correction. Even a mode whose eigenvalue has modulus strictly between $\Theta$ and $1$ decays too slowly. The generalized eigenspaces outside the circle together have finite dimension. More precisely, let $\kappa\in(0,\tfrac14)$ be defined by $\Theta=e^{-\kappa S}$. We solve the equation linearized about $u^*$ in the space of the perturbations $v$ with $$
\sup_{0\le t<1}\,(1-t)^{\frac14-\kappa}\,\|v(t)\|_{\dot H^1}<\infty,
$$ which are those of size $e^{-\kappa s}$ in self-similar variables, and we leave the datum of $v$ free in a finite-dimensional space $E$, a complement of the invariant subspace of $\mathcal M$ on which its powers decay faster than $\Theta^n$. On the fast-decaying subspace one can sum the forcing from the initial period forwards. On the complementary subspace the required decay fixes the initial component through a sum over all future periods. The summable power bounds (4.11) control the two sums and give the right inverse (4.8) of Proposition 4.3. To realize the correction by compactly supported data, choose smooth solenoidal test fields whose projections form a basis of the complement. Their span is $E$ (Subsection 4.4). A contraction then gives, for every $w_0$ in a ball of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ about $u^*(0)=W(0,\cdot)$, an element $\gamma$ of $E$ and a solution $u$ on $[0,1)$ with datum $w_0+\gamma$ such that $u-u^*$ lies in this space. We modulate neither the blow-up time, nor the location of the blow-up, nor the phase of $u^*$ in its period.

We assume nothing about these eigenvalues. In the program of \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] for non-uniqueness an unstable eigenvalue is the hypothesis, and in \[[17](#cite-ref17)\] the main difficulty is to construct a solution that has one. For blow-up it suffices that the eigenvalues outside the disc are finitely many: each of them, whatever its modulus, is removed by a correction of the datum in a finite-dimensional space. More precisely, let $\kappa\in(0,\tfrac14)$ be defined by $\Theta=e^{-\kappa S}$. We solve the equation linearized about $u^*$ in the space of the perturbations $v$ with $$
\sup_{0\le t<1}\,(1-t)^{\frac14-\kappa}\,\|v(t)\|_{\dot H^1}<\infty,
$$ which are those of size $e^{-\kappa s}$ in self-similar variables, and we leave the datum of $v$ free in a finite-dimensional space $E$, a complement of the invariant subspace of $\mathcal M$ on which its powers decay faster than $\Theta^n$. A Lyapunov–Perron argument over the periods of $u^*$ gives a bounded right inverse of this linear problem (Section 4). Since the smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free fields are dense in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, we can choose $E$ among them, and we need not know the regularity or the decay of the eigenfunctions of $\mathcal M$. A contraction then gives, for every $w_0$ in a ball of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ about $u^*(0)=W(0,\cdot)$, an element $\gamma$ of $E$ and a solution $u$ on $[0,1)$ with datum $w_0+\gamma$ such that $u-u^*$ lies in this space. We modulate neither the blow-up time, nor the location of the blow-up, nor the phase of $u^*$ in its period.

changes.adapted_text: For $w_0$ we take the field $u^*(0)$, cut off far from the origin. The cutoff is applied to a vector potential, so that the field remains divergence-free: for $0\le t<1$ and a radius $r>0$ we let $\bar u(t)=\operatorname{curl}\bigl(\eta(\cdot/r)\,A(t)\bigr)$, where $A(t)$ is the vector potential of $u^*(t)$ given in (5.1) and $\eta$ is a smooth cutoff that equals $1$ on $B_{1/2}$ and vanishes outside $B_1$. The field $\bar u(t)$ equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{r/2}$ and vanishes outside $B_r$, and by (1.3) its distance from $u^*(t)$ in $\dot H^1$ is at most a constant multiple of $r^{-1/2}$, uniformly in $t$ (Lemma 5.1). On $\mathbb R^3$ choose $r$ so that $Cr^{-1/2}\le\varepsilon_0$, the permitted distance from $W(0)$ in Proposition 2.1, and take $w_0=\bar u(0)$ (Subsection 5.2). Thus on $\mathbb R^3$ only the datum is cut off; the solution $u^*$ itself, which need not have finite energy, is not. In \[[17](#cite-ref17), §19, p. 75\] the datum is truncated in the same way, through the same potential. Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65), §5, preprint pp. 20–21\], for the Navier–Stokes equations forward in time, and Elgindi, Ghoul and Masmoudi \[[48](#cite-ref48), Subsection 2.6\], for the Euler equations, pass likewise from self-similar solutions of infinite energy to data of finite energy, by a cutoff at a large radius which changes the datum little in the norm in which the solution is perturbed.

changes.adapted_text: On $\mathbb T^3$ we construct the solution for a small blow-up time $T$. By the scaling of the equations this is the same as a large period at the blow-up time $1$: if $u$ solves the equations on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3/L\mathbb Z^3$, then $L\,u(L^2 t,Lx)$ solves them on $[0,L^{-2})\times\mathbb T^3$. We therefore keep the solution $u^*$ and the blow-up time $1$, and we take the period $L=T^{-1/2}$ large. The solution $u^*$ is not periodic, so that on the torus there is no exact solution about which to linearize, and no monodromy operator. We cut the field $u^*$ off at the radius $r=L/8$ and extend it periodically: the approximate solution is $u^{\mathrm a}(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^3}\bar u(t,\cdot-Lj)$, where $\bar u(t)$ is the cutoff field above for this radius, which equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{L/16}$ and vanishes outside $B_{L/8}$. On divergences the heat flow composed with the Leray projection is the convolution with a kernel that decays like $|x|^{-4}$, uniformly in time. The nonlinear term is a divergence, and so is the datum, since a divergence-free field $f$ is the divergence of $x\otimes f$. For $L\ge1$, Lemma 6.1 bounds the $\dot H^1$ error on a period cell by $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$ at every positive heat time for $F\in W^{1,1}$ supported in $\bar B_{L/8}$. The datum tensor $x\otimes\bar u(0)$ has $L^1$ norm $O(L^3)$ and the nonlinear tensor $\bar u\otimes\bar u$ has norm $O(L)$ (Lemma 5.1). Including the cutoff gives a weighted residual $O(L^{-1/2})$ (Lemma 6.2). For the linearized problem we use that $\bar u(t)$ vanishes outside $B_{L/8}$, so that in the equation linearized about $u^{\mathrm a}$ the term that comes from $u^{\mathrm a}$ involves the perturbation only through its restriction <!-- source-page: 9 --> to this ball. We can therefore solve the linearized equation on $\mathbb R^3$, with the right inverse of the equation linearized about $u^*$, and return to the torus; the map so obtained inverts the equation linearized about $u^{\mathrm a}$ up to an error of order $L^{-1/2}$. Choose $L$ so that the error operator has norm at most $1/2$; its Neumann series converges and yields an exact right inverse (Lemma 6.3 and (6.16)). The same contraction as on $\mathbb R^3$ then gives a solution $u$ on the torus of period $L$, and $u_{\mathrm{per}}(t,x)=L\,u(L^2 t,Lx)$ is the solution of Theorem 1.1.

changes.adapted_text: In the proof of Theorem 7.1 we correct an approximate profile to an exact one. Writing $\theta=s/S$ makes the period one and replaces $\partial_s$ by $S^{-1}\partial_\theta$; the unknown period is now a coefficient of the equation. The equation linearized about a time-periodic solution need not be invertible: it has, for instance, the derivative of the solution in time in its kernel. We therefore add to the first equation of (1.2) a force term with finitely many unknown coefficients and impose as many linear constraints on the solution. The certificate estimate gives injectivity of the constrained operator. After a change of unknown it is identity plus compact; the Fredholm alternative gives surjectivity, and the same estimate bounds the inverse (Proposition 7.8). Schauder–Tychonoff gives a fixed point in the product of the compact convex parameter set and a weakly compact ball of right-hand sides. The map subtracts an invertible matrix times the total force coefficients from the parameter (7.30), then projects onto the parameter set. At a fixed point (7.61) puts the trial value in that set. Projection leaves it unchanged, so the parameter step and all total force coefficients vanish (Proposition 7.10). Proposition 7.11 gives smoothness. The velocity is discretely self-similar with $R=I$ and, by continuity in $X$, Sobolev embedding (3.1) and continuity of dilations, is continuous in time into $L^6$ (Subsection 7.10). These are the hypotheses of Chae and Wolf \[[26](#cite-ref26), Theorem 1.1, preprint p. 2\], which gives the Type I bound.
changes.authors_text: In the proof of Theorem 7.1 we correct an approximate profile to an exact one. Since the period of a profile is not known in advance, we rescale the self-similar time, so that the period becomes a coefficient of the equation. The equation linearized about a time-periodic solution need not be invertible: it has, for instance, the derivative of the solution in time in its kernel. We therefore add to the first equation of (1.2) a force term with finitely many unknown coefficients and impose as many linear constraints on the solution. With the Fredholm alternative, the a priori estimate of a certificate gives a bounded inverse of the linearized problem with constraints. The approximate profiles depend on as many parameters as the force term has coefficients, and the remaining conditions bound these coefficients so sharply that the Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem, applied to the parameters and to the quadratic term together, gives a value of the parameters and a solution close to the approximate profile for which the force term vanishes. We then show that this solution is smooth (Proposition 7.11), and since its isometry is the identity, the theorem of Chae and Wolf recalled in Subsection 1.2 gives the Type I bound.

changes.note: Condenses the roadmap while preserving every section and appendix role, leaving space for the local mathematical explanations.
changes.adapted_text: Sections 2–6 prove Theorem 1.1 from a profile. Section 3 supplies the heat estimates, Section 4 the linearized inverse and contraction, and Sections 5–6 the whole-space and torus constructions. Appendix A proves the auxiliary lemmas, including smoothness (Lemma 2.3). Section 7 can be read after Section 3. It constructs the profile from a certificate. Appendix B gives the finite-data conditions implying the required perturbation estimates and Appendix C the numerical construction.
changes.authors_text: In Section 2 we reduce Theorem 1.1 to Propositions 2.1 and 2.2, on $\mathbb R^3$ and on the torus, and to Lemma 2.3 on smooth data. Section 3 contains the properties of the heat flow and of the bilinear term that the rest of the paper uses; most of its proofs, and that of Lemma 2.3, are in Appendix A. In Section 4 we construct the right inverse of the equation linearized about $u^*$ and prove the lemma by which a contraction corrects an approximate solution. In Section 5 we prove Proposition 2.1, and in Section 6 Proposition 2.2. In Section 7, which can be read after Section 3, we define a certificate and prove Theorem 7.1. In Appendix B we describe the form that the formalization prescribes for the data of a certificate, and we derive the estimates that a certificate assumes for every perturbation from conditions on finitely many functions and numbers, attached to data of this form. In Appendix C we describe the numerical computation of the field from which the approximate profiles of the certificate of Subsection 1.1 are formed, and of further fields of this certificate.

For a smooth solution with periodic velocity, (1.1) makes the pressure gradient periodic, so $p(t,x)-b(t)\cdot x$ is periodic for some vector $b(t)$. Passing to a frame of acceleration $-b(t)$ with zero initial displacement and velocity preserves the datum and gives periodic pressure, as Fefferman requires \[[53](#cite-ref53), Errata, unnumbered PDF p. 6\].

The formal proof of the two nonexistence conclusions on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\mathbb T^3$ starts from the finite-data conditions in Appendix B.
changes.authors_text: The formalization also derives the conclusion of the formal Theorem 1.1, on $\mathbb R^3$ and on $\mathbb T^3$, from conditions on finitely many functions and numbers, which do not include the estimates that a certificate assumes for every perturbation. We describe these conditions in Appendix B. The formalization contains no data: that the certificate of Subsection 1.1 satisfies them is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic, which is not part of the formalization.

changes.adapted_text:
Let $B$ be a ball that contains the support of $\varphi$. For $v\in X$ the matrix field $F_v=\varphi\otimes v+v\otimes\varphi$ vanishes outside $B$, and $\operatorname{div}F_v=(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi+(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v$, because $v$ and $\varphi$ are divergence-free; thus $K(\tau)(\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12\,e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}F_v$. Since $|\widehat{\operatorname{div}F_v}(\xi)|\le2\pi|\xi|\,|\hat F_v(\xi)|$ and $16\pi^4|\xi|^4e^{-8\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\le\tau^{-2}$, the definition (2.2), the last identity of (3.2) and Plancherel’s identity give $$
\|K(\tau)(\varphi,v)\|_{\dot H^1}^2=\frac14\int 4\pi^2|\xi|^2e^{-8\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\bigl|\mathbb P_\xi\widehat{\operatorname{div}F_v}(\xi)\bigr|^2\,d\xi\le\frac{\|F_v\|_{L^2}^2}{4\,\tau^2}\le\frac{\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}^2\|v\|_{L^2(B)}^2}{\tau^2}.
$$ Only the values on $B$ enter the last bound. By (3.1) and $\|v\|_{L^2(B)}\le |B|^{1/3}\|v\|_6$, restriction to $B$ is continuous from $X$ to $H^1(B)$, so $v_k\rightharpoonup0$ there. Rellich’s theorem on the bounded ball gives compactness in $L^2(B)$ \[[14](#cite-ref14), Theorem 9.16, p. 285\]. Every subsequence thus has a further subsequence converging strongly to its weak limit, zero. The last bound now gives convergence of $K(\tau)(\varphi,v_k)$ in $X$. $\square$

For $v\in X$ the matrix field $F_v=\varphi\otimes v+v\otimes\varphi$ vanishes outside $B$, and $\operatorname{div}F_v=(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi+(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v$, because $v$ and $\varphi$ are divergence-free; thus $K(\tau)(\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12\,e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}F_v$. \|K(\tau)(\varphi,v)\|_{\dot H^1}^2=\frac14\int 4\pi^2|\xi|^2e^{-8\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\bigl|\mathbb P_\xi\widehat{\operatorname{div}F_v}(\xi)\bigr|^2\,d\xi\le\frac{\|F_v\|_{L^2}^2}{4\,\tau^2}\le\frac{\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}^2\|v\|_{L^2(B)}^2}{\tau^2}.

*Proof.* The bound holds because $\rho_R^{-1}$ is an isometry, $\|D_\lambda\chi\|_{\dot H^1}=\lambda^{1/4}\|\chi\|_{\dot H^1}$ and $\|e^{t_1\Delta}\chi\|_{\dot H^1}\le\|\chi\|_{\dot H^1}$, by (3.5) and (3.3). By (4.9) at time $t_1$ and by (4.10), $$
\mathcal M\chi-\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}\chi=2\,\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda\int_0^{t_1}K(t_1-t')\bigl(u^*(t'),h_\chi(t')\bigr)\,dt'\qquad(\chi\in X).
$$ By the Hilbert-space compactness criterion used in Lemma 3.2, it suffices that the integral tend to $0$ in $X$ for every weakly null sequence $\chi_k$. Such a sequence is bounded. For each $t'\in[0,t_1]$ the map $\chi\mapsto h_\chi(t')$ is linear and bounded, with norm at most $\|\mathcal U\|$, so that $h_{\chi_k}(t')\to0$ weakly. For $t'<t_1$ the <!-- source-page: 19 --> operator $K(t_1-t')(u^*(t'),\cdot)$ is compact (Lemma 3.2), so that the integrand tends to $0$ in $X$ at every $t'<t_1$. By (3.7) its norm is at most $C_K\,(t_1-t')^{-3/4}\,\max_{[0,t_1]}\|u^*\|_{\dot H^1}\,\|\mathcal U\|\,\sup_k\|\chi_k\|_{\dot H^1}$, which is integrable on $[0,t_1]$, and the integral tends to $0$ by dominated convergence. $\square$

*Proof.* We complexify $X$ with $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$. Extending each real operator componentwise preserves its norm, and preserves compactness by applying it to the real and imaginary parts. Thus $\mathcal M$ and $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}$ retain their norms and compact difference. Lemma 4.4 compares one period of the linearized flow with the free heat flow. Buckmaster, Coiculescu and Li use a compact difference of evolution operators over one period in their forward problem \[[17](#cite-ref17), §19, proof of Proposition 19.1\]. Here the norm bound for the free operator is $e^{-S/4}$. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectral radius, so outside this disk the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ consists of isolated poles of finite algebraic multiplicity \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, Paragraph 1.20, pp. 248–249, and (1.16), p. 249\]. For each $r>e^{-S/4}$, compactness of the spectrum allows only finitely many such points with $|z|\ge r$. We can therefore choose $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ so that no spectral point lies on $|z|=\Theta$.

*Proof.* We consider $\mathcal M$ and $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}$ on the complexification of $X$, where they have the same norms and their difference is compact. By Lemma 4.4 the essential spectral radius of $\mathcal M$ is that of $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}$, hence at most $e^{-S/4}$, and therefore every point of the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ of modulus larger than $e^{-S/4}$ is a pole of the resolvent of finite algebraic multiplicity \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, Paragraph 1.20 and (1.16)\]. changes.note: Explains finite rank and descent of the spectral projection to the real Hilbert space, with precise pages. Makes explicit why the strict spectral separation yields summability after the two different weights.
changes.adapted_text: Let $P$ be the Riesz projection for the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$ \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, (1.6)–(1.8), p. 244\]. It commutes with $\mathcal M$ and has finite rank, the sum of the finite algebraic multiplicities \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, Paragraph 1.17, pp. 246–247\]. Complex conjugation commutes with $\mathcal M$ and preserves this spectral set; conjugating the resolvent integral therefore leaves $P$ unchanged. Hence $P$ preserves the real space $X$; denote its restriction by $P_{\mathrm u}$. The spectra of the restrictions of $\mathcal M$ to $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ and to $\operatorname{ran}P$ are the parts of the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ in $\{|z|<\Theta\}$ and in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$. Hence the first restriction has spectral radius less than $\Theta$, and the second is invertible, with an inverse of spectral radius less than $\Theta^{-1}$; in particular $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ is invertible. The spectral radius formula \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter III, Exercise 1.17(2), p. 167\] gives geometric bounds with ratios $r_{\mathrm s}<\Theta$ for forward powers and $r_{\mathrm b}<\Theta^{-1}$ for inverse powers. After the weights in (4.11), their ratios are $r_{\mathrm s}/\Theta<1$ and $\Theta r_{\mathrm b}<1$, so both series converge. $\square$
changes.authors_text: Let $P$ be the Riesz projection of $\mathcal M$ for the part of its spectrum in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$ \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, (1.6)–(1.8)\]. It commutes with $\mathcal M$, it has finite rank \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, Paragraph 1.17\], and it maps $X$ into $X$, because $\mathcal M$ is a real operator and $I-P$ is the integral of $(2\pi i)^{-1}\,(z-\mathcal M)^{-1}$ over the circle $|z|=\Theta$; let $P_{\mathrm u}$ be the restriction of $P$ to $X$. The spectra of the restrictions of $\mathcal M$ to $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ and to $\operatorname{ran}P$ are the parts of the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ in $\{|z|<\Theta\}$ and in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$. Hence the first restriction has spectral radius less than $\Theta$, and the second is invertible, with an inverse of spectral radius less than $\Theta^{-1}$; in particular $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ is invertible. By the spectral radius formula the two series of (4.11) converge. $\square$

*Proof.* Lemma 3.4, with $f=u^*$, gives a continuous solution of (4.12) on each $[0,b]$, $b<1$. Uniqueness makes these solutions agree on overlaps, giving the unique solution on $[0,1)$. The map $v-g$ has the value $\chi$ at time $0$, so that $\chi_0=\chi$. By (4.12) and by (3.13), applied on the same intervals with $u=v-g$, $f=2u^*$ and $h=v$, $$
(v-g)(t)=e^{(t-t_n)\Delta}(v-g)(t_n)+2\int_{t_n}^t K(t-t')(u^*(t'),v(t'))\,dt'\qquad(t_n\le t<1).
$$ We apply $\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}$ to this identity at time $t=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma$. On the left we obtain $v_n(\sigma)-g_n(\sigma)$. In the first term on the right, $\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}e^{\lambda^n\sigma\Delta}=e^{\sigma\Delta}\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}$, by (3.5) and since $\rho_R$ commutes with the heat flow and with the dilations; thus this term becomes $e^{\sigma\Delta}\chi_n$. In the integral we substitute $t'=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma'$. By the last two identities of (3.8) and by (4.3), in the form $\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}u^*(t_n+\lambda^n\sigma')=u^*(\sigma')$, $$
\lambda^n\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}K\bigl(\lambda^n(\sigma-\sigma')\bigr)\bigl(u^*(t'),v(t')\bigr)=K(\sigma-\sigma')\bigl(u^*(\sigma'),v_n(\sigma')\bigr)\qquad(0\le\sigma'<\sigma),
$$ so that the integral becomes $\mathcal B(u^*,v_n)(\sigma)$. Therefore $$
v_n=e^{t\Delta}\chi_n+2\mathcal B(u^*,v_n)+g_n\quad\text{on }[0,t_1],\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad v_n=\mathcal U(e^{t\Delta}\chi_n+g_n)=h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal Ug_n.
$$ Since $t_n+\lambda^nt_1=t_{n+1}$, we have $v_{n+1}(0)=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda v_n(t_1)$ and $g_{n+1}(0)=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda g_n(t_1)$, so that $$
\chi_{n+1}=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda(h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal Ug_n-g_n)(t_1)=\mathcal M\chi_n+f_n,
$$ by (4.10) and the definition (4.13) of $f_n$.

changes.adapted_text: *Proof of Proposition 4.3.* The spectral projection prescribes $P_{\mathrm u}\gamma$, whereas Sections 5 and 6 require $\gamma$ itself to have compact support. We can meet both requirements. Since $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ is dense and $P_{\mathrm u}$ is continuous, its image on this class is dense in $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$. This linear image is closed by finite dimensionality, so every basis vector in the range has a compactly supported smooth solenoidal preimage. Their span $E$ makes $P_{\mathrm u}|_E$ an isomorphism. Its bounded inverse gives $\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\|P_{\mathrm u}\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$. Constants may depend on the fixed choices of $\Theta$, $\kappa$, $P_{\mathrm u}$ and $E$.
changes.authors_text: *Proof of Proposition 4.3.* We first fix $E$. Since $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ is dense in $X$ (Subsection 3.1) and $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$ has finite dimension, $P_{\mathrm u}$ maps $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ onto $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$. We choose fields of $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ that $P_{\mathrm u}$ maps to the elements of a basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$, and we let $E$ be their linear span. Then $P_{\mathrm u}$ maps $E$ isomorphically onto $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$, so that $\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\|P_{\mathrm u}\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$ for $\gamma\in E$. The numbers $\Theta$ and $\kappa$, the projection $P_{\mathrm u}$ and the space $E$ are chosen once, and the constants in $\lesssim$ depend on them.

changes.adapted_text:
Fix $g\in C_\kappa([0,1);X)$. Its forcing terms $f_m$ are independent of the datum (Lemma 4.6). In (4.14), $P_{\mathrm u}f_m$ first contributes to $\chi_{m+1}$. Pull it back $m+1$ periods to time zero. By (4.15) the resulting term has norm $\lesssim\Theta^{m+1}\|\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m+1)}P_{\mathrm u}\|\,\|g\|_\kappa$, so these terms are summable by (4.11). The Lyapunov–Perron choice cancels their sum with $P_{\mathrm u}\gamma$. Since $P_{\mathrm u}|_E$ is an isomorphism, this determines exactly one $\gamma\in E$ with $$
P_{\mathrm u}\gamma=-\sum_{m\ge0}\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m+1)}P_{\mathrm u}f_m,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\|g\|_\kappa.
$$ We take $\chi=\gamma$ in Lemma 4.6. Since $P_{\mathrm u}$ commutes with $\mathcal M$, the recursion gives, by induction on $n$, $$
P_{\mathrm u}\chi_n=-\sum_{m\ge n}\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m-n+1)}P_{\mathrm u}f_m,\qquad
(I-P_{\mathrm u})\chi_n=\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\gamma+\sum_{m<n}\mathcal M^{n-1-m}(I-P_{\mathrm u})f_m.
$$ <!-- source-page: 21 --> We bound the terms of the two sums by (4.15), with $m=n-1+j$ in the first sum and $m=n-1-j$ in the second: $$
\begin{aligned}
\|P_{\mathrm u}\chi_n\|_{\dot H^1}&\lesssim\Theta^{n-1}\|g\|_\kappa\sum_{j\ge1}\Theta^j\|\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-j}P_{\mathrm u}\|,\\
\|(I-P_{\mathrm u})\chi_n\|_{\dot H^1}&\lesssim\|\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\|\,\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}+\Theta^{n-1}\|g\|_\kappa\sum_{0\le j<n}\Theta^{-j}\|\mathcal M^j(I-P_{\mathrm u})\|.
\end{aligned}
$$ By (4.11) the two sums are bounded and $\|\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\|\lesssim\Theta^n$. Thus $\|\chi_n\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\Theta^n\|g\|_\kappa$ for every $n\ge0$.

*Proof.* Fix $r>0$ and $0\le t<1$; all constants below are independent of $r$ and $t$. Differentiation under the integral over $[0,1]$, locally in $(t,x)$ with $t<1$, gives the smoothness of $A$ and $\bar u$. Since $u^*(t)$ is divergence-free, $$
\operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma\,u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x]=\partial_\sigma[\sigma^2\,u^*(t,\sigma x)],
$$ and integration in $\sigma$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A(t)=u^*(t)$: the term at $\sigma=0$ vanishes because of the factor $\sigma^2$. The product rule gives $$
\bar u(t)=\eta(\cdot/r)\,u^*(t)+r^{-1}(\nabla\eta)(\cdot/r)\times A(t).
$$ Thus $\bar u(t)$, which is divergence-free as a curl, equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{r/2}$, where $\eta(\cdot/r)=1$, and vanishes outside $B_r$; in particular it belongs to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$.

We look for a solution in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ on $[0,1)$ of the form $$
u=u^{\mathrm a}+z,\qquad u(0)=u^{\mathrm a}(0)+\Pi_L\gamma,
$$ where $\gamma\in E$ and $z\in C_\kappa([0,1);\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3))$. To form $u^{\mathrm a}$, cut off the vector potential of $u^*$ at radius $L/8$, take its curl, and periodize with $\Pi_L$. The result equals $u^*$ on $B_{L/16}$. Lemma 6.2 bounds the residual in the equation for $u^{\mathrm a}$. Lemma 6.3 bounds the error in using the whole-space right inverse on periodic fields. For large $L$ a convergent series removes this linear error, then Lemma 4.8 corrects the nonlinear residual. Dilation takes the solution to $\mathbb T^3$.

changes.adapted_text:
Let $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $\max_i|x_i|<\frac L2$, let $x'\in\bar B_{L/8}$ and $j\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$. With $|j|_\infty=\max_i|j_i|$ we have $|x-x'-Lj|\ge L\,|j|_\infty-\frac58L\ge\frac38L\,|j|_\infty$, and since $F$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\bar B_{L/8}$, we obtain $$
|h(x-Lj)|\lesssim\bigl(L\,|j|_\infty\bigr)^{-4}\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad|\nabla h(x-Lj)|\lesssim\bigl(L\,|j|_\infty\bigr)^{-5}\|F\|_{L^1}.
$$ There are $O(n^2)$ lattice points with $|j|_\infty=n$. The shells therefore give summable bounds $\lesssim L^{-4}n^{-2}\|F\|_{L^1}$ and $\lesssim L^{-5}n^{-3}\|F\|_{L^1}$. Thus $g_0=\sum_{j\ne0}h(\cdot-Lj)$ and its first derivatives converge uniformly on $\max_i|x_i|<\frac L2$, with $$
|g_0|\lesssim L^{-4}\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad|\nabla g_0|\lesssim L^{-5}\|F\|_{L^1}.
$$ To identify $g_0$, compare Fourier coefficients. Since $h\in L^1$, its periodization has coefficients $L^{-3}\hat h(k)$, where $\hat h(k)=e^{-4\pi^2t|k|^2}\,\mathbb P_k\,\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k)$ by Subsection 3.2. Periodization gives $\operatorname{div}\Pi_LF$ the coefficients $L^{-3}\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k)$, so Subsection 3.6 gives precisely the same coefficients for its projected heat flow. Fourier uniqueness therefore gives $e^{t\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\Pi_LF=h+g_0$, that is, $g=g_0$ and $\nabla g=\nabla g_0$, almost everywhere on the cube. Since the cube has volume $L^3$, the bounds for $g_0$ give $$
\|g\|_{L^6(Q_L)}\lesssim L^{1/2}L^{-4}\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad\|\nabla g\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim L^{3/2}L^{-5}\|F\|_{L^1},
$$ which is (6.2). $\square$

\bar F(t)&=\bar u(t)-e^{t\Delta}\bar u(0)+\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')\bigr)\,dt',\\
F^{\mathrm a}(t)&=\Pi_L\bar u(t)-e^{t\Delta}\Pi_L\bar u(0)+\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\Pi_L\bigl(\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')\bigr)\,dt'.
\end{aligned}
$$ Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; let $0<t<1$. On $Q_L$ the first terms agree. The field $\bar u(0)$ and the matrix fields $\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')$ are smooth and vanish outside $\bar B_{L/8}$. We apply (6.3) to the second terms, and Lemma 6.1 to the third terms under the integrals: $$
\|\nabla\bigl(F^{\mathrm a}(t)-\bar F(t)\bigr)\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim L^{-5/2}\|\bar u(0)\|_{L^1}+L^{-7/2}\int_0^t\|\bar u(t')\|_{L^2}^2\,dt'\lesssim L^{-1/2}.
$$ Here we used (6.4): the norm of $\bar u(0)$ in $L^1$ is at most $|B_{L/8}|^{1/2}\|\bar u(0)\|_{L^2}\lesssim L^2$, and the norm of $\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')$ in $L^1$ is $\|\bar u(t')\|_{L^2}^2\lesssim L$, so that the two terms are at most constant multiples of $L^{-1/2}$ and of $L^{-5/2}$. Since $\|F^{\mathrm a}(t)\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}=\|\nabla F^{\mathrm a}(t)\|_{L^2(Q_L)}$, we conclude that $$
\|F^{\mathrm a}(t)\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}\le\|\bar F(t)\|_{\dot H^1}+\|\nabla\bigl(F^{\mathrm a}(t)-\bar F(t)\bigr)\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}L^{-1/2}+L^{-1/2},
$$ and hence that $\|F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa\lesssim L^{-1/2}$. Finally $F^{\mathrm a}$ takes its values in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ and is continuous on $[0,1)$, by Lemmas 3.7 and 3.3. $\square$

changes.adapted_text: A time-periodic solution can be translated in time without changing its equation. A phase condition fixes this freedom so that the orbit and its period can be found together. For time-periodic Navier–Stokes solutions with a prescribed, time-independent force, \[[90](#cite-ref90), (2.8)–(2.14), pp. 7–9 of the preprint\] treats the frequency as an unknown in a space-time Fourier expansion and fixes the phase. In \[[9](#cite-ref9), (2.14)–(2.15), p. 5\] the phase condition is imposed after rescaling time. Discretely self-similar constructions \[[80](#cite-ref80), Section 1.1, p. 5 of the preprint\], \[[22](#cite-ref22), Section 1.3.1, pp. 4–5\] and the general formulation \[[54](#cite-ref54), Section 3.3, (16)–(17), p. 8 of the preprint\] likewise find the orbit and its frequency or period together near an approximation. Symmetry reduces the unknowns, with sixteen elements in \[[90](#cite-ref90), p. 3, and §5.2, (5.6), p. 43 of the preprint\] and a half-period sign change in \[[22](#cite-ref22), Section 1.3.1, p. 4\]. Here $\Gamma$ includes, for the data described in Subsection B.1 with $\varkappa=19$, a rotation by $\pi/19$ about an axis after half a period and a rotation by $\pi$ about a perpendicular axis. The constraints include the phase choice. Proposition 7.10 selects the correction and $\alpha$, and hence $S(\alpha)$, by a joint Schauder–Tychonoff argument.
changes.authors_text: The computer-assisted constructions of time-periodic solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations with a time-independent force \[[90](#cite-ref90), Section 2\], \[[9](#cite-ref9), Section 2\] and of discretely self-similar solutions \[[80](#cite-ref80)\], \[[22](#cite-ref22), Section 1.3.1\] rescale the time, so that the period, or the frequency, becomes a coefficient of the equation, and impose a condition that removes the translations in time; see also the framework of \[[54](#cite-ref54), Section 3.3\], in which the frequency is an unknown and a phase condition is imposed. In these works the period is found together with the solution, by a fixed point argument around an approximate solution computed numerically, and symmetries reduce the problem, as the set $\Gamma$ does here: a group of sixteen elements in \[[90](#cite-ref90)\], a change of sign after half a period in \[[22](#cite-ref22)\]; for the certificate of Subsection 1.1, a rotation by $\pi/19$ about an axis after half a period and a rotation by $\pi$ about a perpendicular axis (Subsection B.1, with $\varkappa=19$). Here the constraints play the role of the condition on the translations, and the parameter, of which the period $S(\alpha)$ is a given function, is found together with the solution by the Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem (Proposition 7.10).

changes.adapted_text: For Swift–Hohenberg patterns on a two-dimensional torus, \[[89](#cite-ref89), (2.3), p. 4\] also adds a force in a fixed finite span and the same number of constraints. The forcing fields are translation derivatives of the approximate solution. Translation invariance of the energy makes pairing with derivatives of the exact solution a homogeneous linear system for the forcing coefficients; Theorem 2.6, p. 7, of \[[89](#cite-ref89)\] sets those coefficients to zero once its matrix is invertible. Here the pairings with $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ give the bounds following (7.30). For the certificate of Subsection 1.1, one forcing field accounts for time translations and the others are computed directions in which the linearized inverse is largest (Subsection C.4). Donninger and Schörkhuber \[[44](#cite-ref44), Section 2.3, steps (5)–(8), pp. 8–9 of the preprint\] use one parameter for cubic Schrödinger blow-up: they regularize a formal inverse by adding a term along a fixed function, solve the modified equation by contraction at each small parameter, and then use the intermediate value theorem to make its added coefficient vanish. <!-- source-page: 36 -->
changes.authors_text: A force in a fixed finite span, with as many linear constraints, is used in \[[89](#cite-ref89)\] for patterns of the Swift–Hohenberg equation on a two-dimensional torus. There the force lies in the span of the derivatives of an approximate solution in the directions of translation, and its coefficients are shown to vanish by pairing the equation with the derivatives of the solution: by the invariance of the energy under translations, this gives a linear system for the coefficients \[[89](#cite-ref89), Theorem 2.6\], whose matrix is then verified to be invertible. Here the pairing with the fields $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ only bounds the coefficients of the force, as stated after (7.30). In the certificate of Subsection 1.1 only one of the forcing fields accounts for the translations in time; the others were computed as directions in which the inverse of the linearized operator is largest (Subsection C.4). In the construction by Donninger and Schörkhuber \[[44](#cite-ref44), Section 2.3\] of a self-similar blow-up solution of the cubic Schrödinger equation, where there is one parameter, the parameter is found after the solution: a term in the direction of a fixed function is added to a formal inverse of the linearized operator, <!-- source-page: 36 --> the modified equation is solved by a contraction for every small value of the parameter, and the coefficient of the added term vanishes at some value, by the intermediate value theorem.

changes.authors_text: Bounds for the inverse of a linearized operator, of which the a priori estimate (7.18) is an instance, are obtained by computer for stationary problems in several ways: by a decomposition into a coercive part and a compact part approximated by an operator of finite rank, as in \[[62](#cite-ref62), Section 3\] for the Navier–Stokes equations in forward self-similar variables on $\mathbb R^3$, where the strategy of Chen and Hou \[[32](#cite-ref32)\] is followed; by enclosures of eigenvalues, as in \[[95](#cite-ref95), Chapter 3\] for the stationary Navier–Stokes equations on an unbounded strip with an obstacle; and by an approximate inverse built from Fourier series on a box \[[23](#cite-ref23)\].

*Proof.* Set $S=S(\alpha)$ and $\mathcal E(\theta)=\|v(\theta)\|_{\dot H^1}^2$. By Lemma 7.4, $\mathcal E$ is continuous, locally absolutely continuous and period-$1$. The relation for $F$ gives $\mathcal T_Sv=\mathbb P(F-\mathcal C_\alpha v-\sum_i\beta_i b_i)$. Since $\Delta v(\theta)\in L^2_{\mathrm{div}}$ almost everywhere, orthogonality removes $\mathbb P$ from the pairing in (7.42), giving, for almost every $\theta$, $$
 \frac1{2S}\mathcal E'=-\int_{\mathbb R^3}F\cdot\Delta v\,dy+\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i\int_{\mathbb R^3}b_i\cdot\Delta v\,dy-\Bigl[\|\Delta v\|_{L^2}^2+\tfrac14\mathcal E-\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathcal C_\alpha v\cdot\Delta v\,dy\Bigr],
$$ where all fields are taken at time $\theta$. The term in brackets is the left-hand side of (7.22) with $u=v(\theta)$. This $u$ is admissible in (7.22): for almost every $\theta$ it belongs to $X$ and $\Delta u\in L^2$, and <!-- source-page: 41 --> for every $(R,0)\in\Gamma$ the identity $\rho_Rv(\theta)=v(\theta)$ holds for almost every $\theta$, by the $\Gamma$-invariance of $v$, and therefore for every $\theta$, by the continuity of $v$. By (7.22), for almost every $\theta$, $$
 \frac1{2S}\mathcal E'(\theta)\leq\Lambda(\theta),\qquad
 \Lambda(\theta)=\Bigl(\|F(\theta)\|_{L^2}+\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i b_i(\theta)\Bigr\|_{L^2}\Bigr)\|\Delta v(\theta)\|_{L^2}+c_3|v(\theta)|_w^2.
$$ The function $\Lambda$ is nonnegative, since $c_3\geq0$, and has period 1. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, by (7.9) and since $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}\leq\|v\|_w$, $$\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1\Lambda\,d\theta\leq\bigl(\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+b_*|\beta|\bigr)\|v\|_w+c_3\|v\|_w^2.
 \tag{7.56}
\end{equation}$$ Let $\theta_1$ be a point at which $\mathcal E$ attains its minimum. Then $$
 \mathcal E(\theta_1)\leq\int_0^1\mathcal E\,d\theta=\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}^2\leq\frac1{w_*}\|v\|_w^2,
$$ because $w\geq w_*$. The period of $\mathcal E$ is $1/m$. For $m=1$ this is already known. For $m=2$, (7.6) gives $R$ with $(R,\tfrac12)\in\Gamma$, and the $\Gamma$-invariance (7.5) of $v$ gives $v(\theta+\tfrac12)=\rho_Rv(\theta)$, first almost everywhere and then everywhere by continuity; $\rho_R$ preserves the $X$ norm. Thus, for $\theta\in[\theta_1,\theta_1+\frac1m]$, $$
 m\bigl(\mathcal E(\theta)-\mathcal E(\theta_1)\bigr)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\Bigl[\mathcal E\bigl(\theta+\tfrac km\bigr)-\mathcal E\bigl(\theta_1+\tfrac km\bigr)\Bigr]\leq2S\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\int_{\theta_1+k/m}^{\theta+k/m}\Lambda\,d\theta'\leq2S\int_0^1\Lambda\,d\theta',
$$ because the intervals have disjoint interiors, $\Lambda\ge0$, and its integral over any interval of length $1$ is the same. Periodicity of $\mathcal E$ then gives $$
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathbb R}\mathcal E(\theta)\leq\frac1{w_*}\|v\|_w^2+\frac{2S}m\int_0^1\Lambda\,d\theta,
$$ and (7.55) follows from (7.56). $\square$

We check that the solution at $(\alpha,g)$ obeys (7.59), which will also put $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ in $\mathcal Z$. The residual bounds (7.23), the definition of $\mathcal Z$ and (7.17) give $$
 \|F\|_{\mathcal H}\leq\delta(\alpha)+2c_w\varepsilon M,\qquad[F]\leq\delta_0(\alpha)+2c_0c_w\varepsilon M.
$$ Apply the linear estimate (7.52), then the residual inequality (7.24) and the second inequality of (7.21): $$
 \begin{aligned}
 (1-\vartheta)\,\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}&\leq c_1\delta(\alpha)+\delta_0(\alpha)+c_2|\bar\ell(\alpha)|+2(c_1+c_0)c_w\varepsilon M\\
 &\leq(1-\vartheta)\varepsilon+2(1-\vartheta)c_Lc_w\varepsilon M.
 \end{aligned}
$$ Since $\vartheta<1$, division by $1-\vartheta$ and the smallness condition (7.25) yield $$
 \|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\leq\varepsilon(1+2c_Lc_wM)\leq2\varepsilon.
$$ We have $\|v\|_w\leq2\varepsilon$, $|\beta|\leq2\varepsilon/\omega$, $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}\leq\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M$ by (7.23), and $S\leq S_{\max}$. Inserting these in (7.55) and using (7.27) bounds $\sup_\theta\|v(\theta)\|_{\dot H^1}^2$ by $M^2$. Since $M>0$, this proves (7.59). Lemma 7.6 gives $\|(v\cdot\nabla)v\|_{\mathcal H}\leq2c_w\varepsilon M$, and $\Gamma$-invariance of $v$ puts the product in $\mathcal Z$.

We first show that the solution at $(\alpha,g)$ satisfies the bounds (7.59) and that its quadratic term $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ belongs to $\mathcal Z$. By (7.23) and (7.17), $$
 \|F\|_{\mathcal H}\leq\delta(\alpha)+2c_w\varepsilon M,\qquad[F]\leq\delta_0(\alpha)+2c_0c_w\varepsilon M.
$$ By (7.52), then (7.24) and the second condition of (7.21), $$
 \begin{aligned}
 (1-\vartheta)\,\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}&\leq c_1\delta(\alpha)+\delta_0(\alpha)+c_2|\bar\ell(\alpha)|+2(c_1+c_0)c_w\varepsilon M\\
 &\leq(1-\vartheta)\varepsilon+2(1-\vartheta)c_Lc_w\varepsilon M.
 \end{aligned}
$$ We divide by $1-\vartheta>0$ and use (7.25): $$
 \|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\leq\varepsilon(1+2c_Lc_wM)\leq2\varepsilon.
$$ In particular $\|v\|_w\leq2\varepsilon$ and $|\beta|\leq2\varepsilon/\omega$. Moreover $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}\leq\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M$, by (7.23), and $S\leq S_{\max}$. With these bounds, the right-hand side of (7.55) is at most the left-hand side of (7.27), so that $\sup_\theta\|v(\theta)\|_{\dot H^1}\leq M$. These are the bounds (7.59). With them, Lemma 7.6 gives $\|(v\cdot\nabla)v\|_{\mathcal H}\leq2c_w\varepsilon M$, and $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ is $\Gamma$-invariant, because $v$ is. Thus $(v\cdot\nabla)v\in\mathcal Z$.

Let $\mathcal N$ be the nearest-point projection, for the Euclidean norm, onto the nonempty closed convex set $\mathcal K$. It is continuous and fixes every point of $\mathcal K$ \[[14](#cite-ref14), Theorem 5.2, p. 132; Proposition 5.3, p. 134\]. For $(\alpha,g)\in\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ define $$
 \mathcal G(\alpha,g)=\bigl(\mathcal N(\alpha'),\,(v\cdot\nabla)v\bigr),
$$ where $(v,\beta)$ solves (7.57) at $(\alpha,g)$ and $\alpha'$ is given by (7.30). The first component lies in $\mathcal K$ by definition of the projection, and the second lies in $\mathcal Z$ by the preceding bounds. Thus $\mathcal G$ maps $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ into itself.

Let $\mathcal N$ be the nearest-point projection of $\mathbb R^n$ onto the closed convex set $\mathcal K$, for the Euclidean norm; it is continuous, and it is the identity on $\mathcal K$ \[[14](#cite-ref14), Theorem 5.2 and Proposition 5.3\]. For $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and $g\in\mathcal Z$ let $$
 \mathcal G(\alpha,g)=\bigl(\mathcal N(\alpha'),\,(v\cdot\nabla)v\bigr),
$$ where $(v,\beta)$ is the solution at $(\alpha,g)$ and $\alpha'$ is the vector (7.30) formed with this $\beta$. By what we have proved, $\mathcal G$ maps $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ into itself.

changes.adapted_text: Give $\mathcal K$ its Euclidean topology and $\mathcal Z$ its weak topology. The latter is a closed ball in the closed subspace of $\Gamma$-invariant fields in the separable Hilbert space $\mathcal H$. Hence $\mathcal Z$ is weakly compact \[[14](#cite-ref14), Corollary 3.22, p. 71\] and metrizable \[[14](#cite-ref14), Theorem 3.29, p. 74\]. The product $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ is compact, convex and nonempty in $\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal H$ with $\mathcal H$ weak. Schauder–Tychonoff \[[88](#cite-ref88), §2, p. 770\] gives a fixed point once $\mathcal G$ is sequentially continuous. Let $\alpha_k\to\alpha$ and $g_k\rightharpoonup g$ in $\mathcal H$ with pairs in $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ and corresponding solutions $(v_k,\beta_k)$ and $(v,\beta)$. By continuity of $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $\mathcal N$ it suffices to show $\beta_k\to\beta$ and $(v_k\cdot\nabla)v_k\rightharpoonup(v\cdot\nabla)v$ in $\mathcal H$.
replaced: 7.8 The nonlinear problem and the choice of the parameter#8
changes.authors_text: We claim that $\mathcal G$ has a fixed point. The set $\mathcal Z$ is a closed ball of the closed subspace of $\Gamma$-invariant fields in $\mathcal H$. Hence it is convex and compact for the weak topology of $\mathcal H$, and on $\mathcal Z$ this topology is metrizable, because $\mathcal H$ is separable \[[14](#cite-ref14), Corollary 3.22 and Theorem 3.29\]. Thus $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ is a compact convex subset of the locally convex space $\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal H$, in which $\mathcal H$ carries its weak topology, and by the Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem \[[88](#cite-ref88), §2\] every continuous map of such a set into itself has a fixed point. Since the topology of $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ is metrizable, and since $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $\mathcal N$ are continuous, it remains to prove the following. Let $(\alpha_k,g_k)$ and $(\alpha,g)$ be points of $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ such that $\alpha_k\to\alpha$ and $g_k\to g$ weakly in $\mathcal H$, and let $(v_k,\beta_k)$ and $(v,\beta)$ be the solutions at $(\alpha_k,g_k)$ and at $(\alpha,g)$. Then $\beta_k\to\beta$ in $\mathbb R^n$ and $(v_k\cdot\nabla)v_k\to(v\cdot\nabla)v$ weakly in $\mathcal H$.

changes.adapted_text: For (7.39), fix $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$. Equation (7.7) gives $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_RW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta)$ at every $\theta$. Invariance of $v$ gives the same equality almost everywhere in $\theta$ by (7.5). Its two sides are continuous into $X$, so equality extends to every $\theta$. Adding gives $\mathcal W(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_R\mathcal W(\theta)$ and hence $W(s+\theta_0S,\cdot)=\rho_RW(s,\cdot)$ in $X$ for every $s$. Equality in $X$ is equality almost everywhere in space; spatial continuity of $W$ extends it to every $y$, proving (7.39). $\square$
changes.authors_text: It remains to prove (7.39). Let $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$. By (7.7), $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_RW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta)$ for every $\theta$. Since $v$ is $\Gamma$-invariant, $v(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_Rv(\theta)$ for almost every $\theta$, by (7.5), and then for every $\theta$, because both sides are continuous with values in $X$. Hence $\mathcal W(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_R\mathcal W(\theta)$ for every $\theta$, that is, $W(s+\theta_0S,\cdot)=\rho_RW(s,\cdot)$ in $X$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$. Since $W$ is continuous, the two sides are equal at every point, which is (7.39). $\square$

changes.note: Justify compact support after changing variables and expand the passage from a distributional identity to an identity at every time.
changes.adapted_text:
We first prove the mild identity on every $[a,b]$ with $a<b<1$. The local integrability assumptions on $\mathcal W$, the chain rule (7.41) and $(u\cdot\nabla)u(t,x)=e^{3S\theta/2}(\mathcal W\cdot\nabla)\mathcal W(\theta,y)$ give local integrability of $\partial_tu$, $\Delta u$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u$. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty((-\infty,1))$ and $\psi\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$, the transformed test $e^{-S\theta}\phi(t)\psi(x)$ is smooth, divergence-free and compactly supported: the time support stays away from $t=1$. Since $dx\,dt=S e^{-5S\theta/2}\,dy\,d\theta$, testing the weak equation gives $$
 \begin{aligned}
 &\int_{-\infty}^1\phi(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl[\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr]\cdot\psi\,dx\,dt\\
 &\qquad=S\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl[\mathcal T_S\mathcal W+(\mathcal W\cdot\nabla)\mathcal W\bigr](\theta,y)\cdot e^{-S\theta}\phi(t)\,\psi(x)\,dy\,d\theta=0.
 \end{aligned}
$$ Since $u(t)$ is divergence-free, an integration by parts on the left-hand side gives $$
 \int_{-\infty}^1\phi'(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(t)\cdot\psi\,dx\,dt=-\int_{-\infty}^1\phi(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u(t)\cdot\Delta\psi+\bigl(u(t)\otimes u(t)\bigr):\nabla\psi\Bigr]\,dx\,dt.
$$ Both time-dependent pairings are continuous, since $u$ is continuous into $X\hookrightarrow L^6$ and $\psi$ has compact support. The identity says that the distributional derivative of the left pairing is the continuous right pairing in (3.14). Subtracting an antiderivative leaves a distribution with zero derivative, hence a constant. The original continuous pairing is therefore continuously differentiable and satisfies (3.14) at every $t<1$. Lemma 3.6 gives the mild identity on $[a,b]$.

changes.adapted_text: Fix $a<b<1$. By (7.65) and $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{L^1}\lesssim\tau^{-1/2}$ from (3.9), (7.64) converges absolutely pointwise and Fubini identifies it almost everywhere with the $X$-valued integral. Translating $a$ to zero gives the Stokes formula \[[69](#cite-ref69), (3.5), preprint p. 7\] with datum $u(a)$, force $-\sum_m\partial_m(u_m u)$ and kernel $\partial_m(O_\tau)_{ij}$. Thus $u(a+t,x)$ is a bounded mild solution with bounded datum \[[69](#cite-ref69), Section 4, preprint p. 10\]. Proposition 4.1 \[[69](#cite-ref69), preprint p. 11\] bounds the distributional derivatives $(t-a)^{k/2+l}\nabla_x^k\partial_t^l u$ on $(a,b)\times\mathbb R^3$ for all integers $k,l\geq0$. Starting earlier gives bounded derivatives of every order on each compact interval, hence a smooth representative of $u$ on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Its slices represent $u(t)$ in $X$ for every $t$ by continuity from almost every time.
changes.authors_text: We now prove that $u$ is smooth. Let $a<b<1$. By (7.65), $u$ is a bounded measurable function on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, and $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{L^1}\lesssim\tau^{-1/2}$, by (3.9). Hence, for every $t\in(a,b]$, the integral in (7.64) converges absolutely at every point of $\mathbb R^3$, and by Fubini’s theorem (7.64) holds almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^3$ with the integral taken at each point. With the time 0 in place of $a$, this is the formula \[[69](#cite-ref69), (3.5)\] for the solution of the Stokes system with the datum $u(a)$ and the right-hand side $-\sum_m\partial_m(u_m\,u)$: the kernel of that formula is the derivative $\partial_m$ of the kernel of $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P$, that is, $\partial_m(O_\tau)_{ij}$. Thus the bounded function $(t,x)\mapsto u(a+t,x)$ on $(0,b-a)\times\mathbb R^3$ is a mild solution of the Cauchy problem for (1.1) with the bounded datum $u(a)$, in the sense of \[[69](#cite-ref69), Section 4\], and by \[[69](#cite-ref69), Proposition 4.1\], for all integers $k,l\geq0$ the function $(t-a)^{k/2+l}\,\nabla_x^k\partial_t^l u$ is bounded on $(a,b)\times\mathbb R^3$, where the derivatives are taken in the sense of distributions. Since $a<b<1$ are arbitrary, $u$ is equal almost everywhere on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ to a smooth function, all derivatives of which are bounded on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$ whenever $a<b<1$. For every $t<1$ the value of this function at time $t$ is the element $u(t)$ of $X$: this holds for almost every $t$, and both depend continuously on $t$. From now on $u$ denotes this smooth function.

changes.note: Expand the pressure reconstruction directly from solenoidal testing and verify the sign of the displayed radial primitive.
changes.adapted_text:
Set $G=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, which is smooth. Equation (3.14) gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}G(t)\cdot\psi\,dx=0$ for every compactly supported solenoidal test $\psi$ and every $t<1$. Taking $\psi$ to be the curl of a compactly supported smooth field gives $\operatorname{curl}G(t)=0$. The radial primitive on $\mathbb R^3$ then gives $G=-\nabla p$ with $$
 p(t,x)=-\int_0^1G(t,\sigma x)\cdot x\,d\sigma,
$$ which is smooth in $(t,x)$. To check the gradient, use $\partial_iG_j=\partial_jG_i$ and differentiate under the integral: the resulting integrand is $\partial_\sigma(\sigma G_i(t,\sigma x))$. Thus $\partial_i p=-G_i$, and $(u,p)$ satisfies (1.1) throughout $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$.
changes.authors_text:
We turn to the pressure. Let $G=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, a smooth field on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Since $u$ is smooth, the identity (3.14) gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}G(t)\cdot\psi\,dx=0$ for every $t<1$ and every $\psi\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$, so that $\operatorname{curl}G(t)=0$ and $G=-\nabla p$ with $$
 p(t,x)=-\int_0^1G(t,\sigma x)\cdot x\,d\sigma,
$$ a smooth function on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Thus the smooth functions $u$ and $p$ satisfy (1.1) on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$.

adapted: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#2
changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.4.* For $\beta>0$, equip $C([a,b];\mathcal X)$ with $\|h\|_\beta=\max_{a\leq t\leq b}e^{-\beta(t-a)}\|h(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$, an equivalent complete norm. Let $Lh$ denote the integral term in the lemma. Lemma 3.3 gives $Lh\in C([a,b];\mathcal X)$. By (3.12) and $e^{-\beta(t-a)}=e^{-\beta(t-t')}e^{-\beta(t'-a)}$, its operator norm is at most $$
 2C_K\max_{[a,b]}\|f\|_{\mathcal X}\int_0^\infty\tau^{-3/4}e^{-\beta\tau}\,d\tau,
$$ where the substitution $s=\beta\tau$ makes the integral a finite constant times $\beta^{-1/4}$. Choose $\beta$ so that $\|L\|_\beta<1$. Then $h\mapsto Lh+g$ has a unique fixed point, and the convergent series $(I-L)^{-1}=\sum_{j\geq0}L^j$ shows that $g\mapsto h$ is linear and bounded. Equivalence of norms gives the asserted supremum-norm bound. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.4.* For $\beta>0$ we give the space of continuous maps $h:[a,b]\to\mathcal X$ the norm $\max_{a\leq t\leq b}e^{-\beta(t-a)}\|h(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$, which is equivalent to the supremum norm. By Lemma 3.3 the integral term of the equation of the lemma defines a linear map of this space into itself, and since $e^{-\beta(t-a)}=e^{-\beta(t-t')}e^{-\beta(t'-a)}$, the bound of (3.12) shows that the norm of this map is at most $$
 2C_K\max_{[a,b]}\|f\|_{\mathcal X}\int_0^\infty\tau^{-3/4}e^{-\beta\tau}\,d\tau,
$$ where the integral is a constant multiple of $\beta^{-1/4}$. For $\beta$ large the map is a contraction, which gives the lemma. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.5.* Apply $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ to the identity at time $m$. This bounded linear operator commutes with the Bochner integral, which is integrable by Lemma 3.3. The semigroup law (3.11) and the first identity in (3.12) give $$
 e^{(t-m)\Delta}u(m)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))\,dt',
$$ and subtracting this from the identity at $t$, then splitting the integral at $m$, gives (3.13). For uniqueness, suppose $u(a)=v(a)$. Symmetry and bilinearity give $K(\tau)(u,u)-K(\tau)(v,v)=K(\tau)(u+v,u-v)$. Thus $u-v$ satisfies Lemma 3.4 with $f=(u+v)/2$ and $g=0$. Its unique solution is zero. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.5.* We apply the bounded operator $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ to the identity for $u$ at time $m$. By (3.11) and the first identity of (3.12), $$
 e^{(t-m)\Delta}u(m)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))\,dt',
$$ and subtracting this from the identity at time $t$ gives (3.13). For the uniqueness, let $u$ and $v$ be two solutions on $[a,b]$ with $u(a)=v(a)$. Since $K$ is bilinear and symmetric, the difference $u-v$ satisfies the equation of Lemma 3.4 with $\frac12(u+v)$ in place of $f$ and with $g=0$, and hence $u=v$. $\square$

changes.note: States the local square integrability required by Dubois and explains the passage from fixed spatial tests to time-dependent tests and from a distributional to an X-valued integral.
adapted: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#4
changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.6.* Translate time to set $a=0$. Let $E_2$ be the closure of the Schwartz functions in $\sup_x\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}$ \[[46](#cite-ref46), p. 29\]. Hölder’s inequality gives $\sup_x\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^6}$; approximation by $C_c^\infty$ therefore embeds $L^6$ continuously in $E_2$. By (3.1), $u\in C([0,b];E_2)$, hence $u\in L^2((0,m);E_2)$ for each $m<b$, as Dubois’s theorem requires. Let $\varphi$ be a smooth compactly supported field on $[0,m]\times\mathbb R^3$, divergence-free at each time. To differentiate $\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)$, split its increment into the change in $u$ with the test fixed and the change in the test. Apply (3.14) to the first part and continuity of $u$ in $L^6$ to the second. This gives the continuous derivative <!-- source-page: 48 --> $$
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u\cdot\bigl(\partial_t\varphi+\Delta\varphi\bigr)+\bigl(u\otimes u\bigr):\nabla\varphi\Bigr]\,dx.
$$ Integration from $0$ to $m$ gives Dubois’s formulation (NSW) at time $m$, with datum $u(0)$ \[[46](#cite-ref46), p. 29\], so $u$ solves (NSW) on $(0,b)$. Theorem 1 of \[[46](#cite-ref46), pp. 29–30\] then supplies a tempered distribution $v_0$ such that $$
 u(t)=e^{t\Delta}v_0-\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(u(t')\otimes u(t')\bigr)\,dt'\qquad(0\leq t<b)
$$ in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^3)$. Its continuous trace at $t=0$ gives $v_0=u(0)$. Since $u(t')\in L^6$, $\nabla u(t')\in L^2$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, Hölder’s inequality gives $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)=(u\cdot\nabla)u\in L^{3/2}$. By (2.2)–(2.3), the integrand after the minus sign is $-K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$. Lemma 3.3 gives its integral in $X$; testing against Schwartz fields, which act continuously on $X$ by (3.1), identifies it with the distributional integral. This proves (2.4) for $t<b$. Continuity of both sides in $X$, from Subsection 3.1 and Lemma 3.3, includes $t=b$. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.6.* Translating the time, we may assume that $a=0$. Let $E_2$ be the space of \[[46](#cite-ref46)\], the closure of the Schwartz functions on $\mathbb R^3$ in the norm $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}$. Since $\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^6}$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ is dense in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, this space contains $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, and by (3.1) $u$ is a continuous map from $[0,b]$ to $E_2$. Let $0<m<b$, and let $\varphi$ be a smooth, compactly supported field on $[0,m]\times\mathbb R^3$ that is divergence-free at each time. Since $u$ is continuous with <!-- source-page: 48 --> values in $L^6$, the hypothesis (3.14) for the fields $\psi=\varphi(t)$ and the product rule show that the function $t\mapsto\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)\,dx$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,m]$, with the derivative $$
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u\cdot\bigl(\partial_t\varphi+\Delta\varphi\bigr)+\bigl(u\otimes u\bigr):\nabla\varphi\Bigr]\,dx.
$$ Integrating from 0 to $m$, we obtain the identity of the formulation (NSW) of \[[46](#cite-ref46)\] at the time $m$, with the datum $u(0)$; the fields $\varphi$ above are the test fields of that formulation. Thus $u$ is a solution of (NSW) on $(0,b)$, and by \[[46](#cite-ref46), Theorem 1\] there is a tempered distribution $v_0$ such that $$
 u(t)=e^{t\Delta}v_0-\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(u(t')\otimes u(t')\bigr)\,dt'\qquad(0\leq t<b)
$$ in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^3)$. At $t=0$ this gives $v_0=u(0)$. The field $\operatorname{div}(u(t')\otimes u(t'))=(u(t')\cdot\nabla)u(t')$ belongs to $L^{3/2}$, so that the integrand is $-K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$, by (2.2) and (2.3), and since the Schwartz fields are continuous linear functionals on $X$, by (3.1), the integral is that of (2.4). Thus (2.4) holds for $0\leq t<b$, and it holds at $t=b$ because both of its sides are continuous on $[0,b]$ with values in $X$ (Subsection 3.1 and Lemma 3.3). $\square$

changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.7.* Let $L>0$ and $\tau>0$, let $f\in L^{3/2}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ have mean zero, and let $z=e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf$. Since $|\hat z(k)|\leq e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}L^{-3}\|f\|_{L^1(Q_L)}$, the field $z$ is smooth; it is real and divergence-free, and it has mean zero. Thus $z$ belongs to $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$, and so does the field $\Psi=-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}z$, whose Fourier coefficients are $4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)$. Since $\mathbb P_k$ is a real symmetric matrix and $\mathbb P_k\hat z(k)=\hat z(k)$, Parseval’s identity and (3.15) give $$
 \int_{Q_L}\Psi\cdot f\,dx=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)\cdot\overline{\hat f(k)}=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2|\hat z(k)|^2=\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2.
$$ Since $4\pi^2|k|^2\leq\tau^{-1}e^{4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}$, the norms of $\Psi$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and in $\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$ are at most $\tau^{-1/2}$ and $\tau^{-1}$ times $\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}$. By Hölder’s inequality and (3.18) for $\Psi$, $$
 \|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2\leq\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|\Psi\|_{L^2(Q_L)}^{1/2}\|\Psi\|_{L^6(Q_L)}^{1/2}\lesssim\tau^{-3/4}\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)},
$$ which gives (3.19), immediately if $z=0$ and otherwise by division by $\|z\|_{\dot H^1}$. The identity $e^{t\Delta}e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf=e^{(t+\tau)\Delta}\mathbb Pf$ holds coefficient by coefficient. For continuity at $\tau_0>0$, write the field near $\tau_0$ as $e^{(\tau-\tau_0/2)\Delta}(e^{(\tau_0/2)\Delta}\mathbb Pf)$. The inner field lies in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$, so strong continuity of the heat flow applies from both sides of $\tau_0$.

*Proof of Lemma 3.7.* Let $L>0$ and $\tau>0$, let $f\in L^{3/2}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ have mean zero, and let $z=e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf$. Since $|\hat z(k)|\leq e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}L^{-3}\|f\|_{L^1(Q_L)}$, the field $z$ is smooth; it is real and divergence-free, and it has mean zero. Thus $z$ belongs to $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$, and so does the field $\Psi=-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}z$, whose Fourier coefficients are $4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)$. Since $\mathbb P_k$ is a real symmetric matrix and $\mathbb P_k\hat z(k)=\hat z(k)$, Parseval’s identity and (3.15) give $$
 \int_{Q_L}\Psi\cdot f\,dx=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)\cdot\overline{\hat f(k)}=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2|\hat z(k)|^2=\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2.
$$ Since $4\pi^2|k|^2\leq\tau^{-1}e^{4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}$, the norms of $\Psi$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and in $\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$ are at most $\tau^{-1/2}$ and $\tau^{-1}$ times $\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}$. By Hölder’s inequality and (3.18) for $\Psi$, $$
 \|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2\leq\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|\Psi\|_{L^2(Q_L)}^{1/2}\|\Psi\|_{L^6(Q_L)}^{1/2}\lesssim\tau^{-3/4}\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)},
$$ which gives (3.19). The identity $e^{t\Delta}e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf=e^{(t+\tau)\Delta}\mathbb Pf$ holds coefficient by coefficient, and with it the continuity in $\tau$ follows from that of the heat flow on $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$.

changes.note: Identifies Tao’s unforced local mild-solution spaces, the pressure convention, and the continuation corollaries.
changes.adapted_text: Tao’s unforced $H^1$ theory takes solenoidal $H^1$ data and gives a local mild solution in $L^\infty_tH^1_x\cap L^2_tH^2_x$ with pressure determined by the velocity \[[84](#cite-ref84), published pp. 29, 31, (9), (11)\]. Corollaries 5.2 and 5.8 give the continuation alternatives.
changes.authors_text: We deduce the lemma from the local theory in $H^1$, in the form given by Tao \[[84](#cite-ref84), Section 5\], which concerns solutions in a smaller class. An $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ in the sense of \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 31\], without force and with a divergence-free datum $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, is a divergence-free field $\tilde u\in L^\infty([0,b];H^1(\mathbb R^3))\cap L^2([0,b];H^2(\mathbb R^3))$ which satisfies the integral equation \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] with the datum $u_0$; its pressure $\tilde p$ is determined by $\tilde u(t)$ at each time $t$, through the formula \[[84](#cite-ref84), (9)\]. The periodic $H^1$ mild solutions of \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 29\] are defined in the same way on the torus. We show that such a solution with the datum $u(0)$ coincides with $u$ as long as it exists, and that its norm in $H^1$ remains bounded. By the alternative of \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] between existence and blow-up in $H^1$, it then exists on $[0,b]$ for every $b<T$, and $u$ has the smoothness that \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] proves in this class.
