*Proof of Lemma 2.3.* Let $u$ satisfy the first assertion, set $u_0=u(0)$ and fix $0<b<T$. Obtain a local $H^1$ mild solution $\tilde u$ from $u_0$ on $[0,b']$, $0<b'\leq b$, by \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(ii)\]. By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i)\], $\tilde u$ is continuous in $H^1$ and hence in $X$ by solenoidality and $H^1\subset L^6$. Lemma 3.3 integrates $K(t-t')(\tilde u(t'),\tilde u(t'))$ from \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] in $X$, continuously in $t$. Schwartz tests identify the distributional integral, and continuity in $X$ extends the identity to every time. Lemma 3.5 gives $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$. Since $u_0\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ is Schwartz, $\tilde u,\tilde p$ are smooth on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$ with every time and space derivative bounded in $L^2$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(iv)\]. Equation (10) of \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] gives (1.1). Testing with $\tilde u$ and integrating by parts gives $\frac d{dt}\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=-2\|\nabla\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2$, since solenoidality cancels pressure and transport. Thus $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}$ and $$
 \|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}+\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\qquad(0\leq t\leq b').
$$ Continuity of $u$ into $X$ on $[0,b]$ bounds the right side independently of $b'$. By Corollary 5.8 of \[[84](#cite-ref84)\], an $H^1$ mild solution exists on $[0,b]$ unless some $T_*\in(0,b]$ has $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ as $t\to T_*$. The same bound on all $[0,b']$ with $b'<T_*$ rules this out. The smooth solution thus agrees with $u$ on $[0,b]$ and has $L^2$ norm at most $\|u_0\|_{L^2}$, for arbitrary $b<T$.
changes.authors_text:
*Proof of Lemma 2.3.* Let $u$ be as in the first assertion, let $u_0=u(0)$ and $0<b<T$, and let $\tilde u$ be an $H^1$ mild solution on an interval $[0,b']$, $0<b'\leq b$, with datum $u_0$. By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i)\] it is a continuous map from $[0,b']$ to $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and since its values are divergence-free and $H^1(\mathbb R^3)\subset L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, it is a continuous map from $[0,b']$ to $X$. Since $\operatorname{div}\tilde u=0$, the integrand of \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] is $K(t-t')(\tilde u(t'),\tilde u(t'))$, so that the integral converges in $X$ as well, to the same field, and is continuous in $t$ with values in $X$, by Lemma 3.3. Both sides of the equation are therefore continuous in $t$ with values in $X$, so that it holds at every time. Thus $\tilde u$ is a mild solution on $[0,b']$, and $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$, by Lemma 3.5. Moreover, $u_0$ is a Schwartz field. Hence $\tilde u$ and $\tilde p$ are smooth on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$, and all their derivatives in $t$ and $x$ are bounded on $[0,b']$ with values in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(iv)\]. The formula \[[84](#cite-ref84), (10)\] is the integral form of (1.1), so that $(\tilde u,\tilde p)$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$ with datum $u_0$. By these bounds we may multiply (1.1) by $\tilde u$ and integrate by parts over $\mathbb R^3$, which gives $\frac d{dt}\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=-2\|\nabla\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2\leq0$. Hence $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}$ and, since $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$, $$
 \|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}+\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\qquad(0\leq t\leq b').
$$ By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.8\], either there is an $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ with datum $u_0$, or there are $T_*\in(0,b]$ and a map $\tilde u$ from $[0,T_*)$ to $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ as $t\to T_*$, whose restriction to $[0,b']$ is an $H^1$ mild solution with datum $u_0$ for every $b'<T_*$. The second case does not occur, because the bound above holds on $[0,b']$ for every $b'<T_*$. Hence there is an $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ with datum $u_0$. As we have shown, it is the restriction of $u$ to $[0,b]$, it is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, and its norm in $L^2$ does not exceed that of $u_0$. Since $b<T$ is arbitrary, this proves the first assertion.

changes.adapted_text: For smooth mean-zero solenoidal $u_0$ on $\mathbb T^3$, apply the periodic $H^1$ theory \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i),(ii),(iv)\] with $K_{\mathbb T}$ replacing $K$. Continuity in $H^1$ and preservation of the mean \[[84](#cite-ref84), (39)\] give continuity in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T^3)$. Lemma 3.7 permits the use of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5, identifying this velocity with $u$. If the alternative \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.2\] gave blow-up at $T_*\leq b<T$, (3.16) would give $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\lesssim\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$ for $t<T_*$, excluding blow-up. The solution is therefore smooth on $[0,b]$ by Theorem 5.1(iv), with periodic pressure by the periodic $H^1$ definition \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 29\]. This holds for every $b<T$. $\square$
changes.authors_text: Now let $u$ be as in the second assertion, with the smooth datum $u_0$, and let $0<b<T$. The argument is the same, with the periodic $H^1$ mild solutions, whose velocity and pressure are periodic, with $K_{\mathbb T}$ in place of $K$, and with \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i) and (iv) and Corollary 5.2\] in place of \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i) and (iv) and Corollary 5.8\]. The datum has mean zero, as the theory on the torus requires \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1\]. A periodic $H^1$ mild solution with this datum is a continuous map into $H^1(\mathbb T^3)$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i)\] whose values are divergence-free and have mean zero \[[84](#cite-ref84), (39)\], and hence a continuous map into $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T^3)$, and Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5 apply in this space by Lemma 3.7. The second case of \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.2\] does not occur: in that case $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,T_*)$, and $\|u(t)\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\lesssim\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T^3)}$ for $0\leq t<T_*$, by (3.16). Hence the restriction of $u$ to $[0,b]$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b]\times\mathbb T^3$, and since $b<T$ is arbitrary, this proves the second assertion. $\square$

changes.adapted_text: Section 7 needs estimates valid for every admissible perturbation. Here the input consists of finitely many represented functions, matrices and numbers. Proposition B.1 tests the linearized equation against a multiplier. Proposition B.4 estimates the resulting quadratic form on the cells of the meridian plane. The exterior estimates and the tree of matrices in Subsection B.3 complete the bound (7.18). Subsection B.4 obtains (7.19), (7.22) and (7.32)–(7.34) and lists the conditions imposed directly. Proposition B.14 then gives the Section 7 certificate under all these conditions, including those specified after its proof. Appendix C explains the radial phase and the choice of weights. <!-- source-page: 50 -->

changes.authors_text: In this appendix we describe the form that the formalization (Subsection 1.5) prescribes for the data of a certificate, and we derive, from conditions on finitely many functions and numbers attached to data of this form, the estimates (7.18), (7.19) and (7.22) and the bounds (7.32) to (7.34). The result is Proposition B.14: data of this form that satisfy these conditions are a certificate in the sense of Section 7. We prove it here except for two statements, whose proofs are in the formalization and which we only describe: Proposition B.1, the inequality for a multiplier with which the a priori estimate (7.18) begins (Subsection B.2), and Proposition B.4, the inequalities for the cells of a mesh of the meridian plane, from which the rest of this estimate is assembled along a tree of matrices (Subsection B.3). In the formalization the two are stated for larger classes of perturbations and of right-hand sides. By the conditions of this appendix we mean those of Subsections B.1 to B.4 together with the further ones that are named after <!-- source-page: 50 --> Proposition B.14; together they are the hypothesis of the formal statement. The radial phase of Subsection B.1 and the weights of Subsection B.2 are explained in Appendix C.

changes.adapted_text: For each amplitude, the $\sigma$ and $\eta$ partitions divide $[0,1]\times[-1,1]$ into rectangles. On each rectangle the amplitude is a complex polynomial. Across a common edge the two polynomial traces agree, as do their derivatives normal to that edge up to the prescribed order. The orders in $(\sigma,\eta)$ are $(2,1)$ for $\mathsf A$, $(1,2)$ for $\mathsf B$, $(2,2)$ for $\mathsf S$ and $(1,1)$ for $\mathsf T$. These matches keep all components of (B.7) and (B.8) continuously differentiable when a derivative in the formulas crosses a partition edge. In addition, $\mathsf S$ and $\mathsf T$ vanish at $\sigma=0$. The field (B.6) is then of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and has period 1 in $\theta$; its second derivatives are bounded functions, which are the classical derivatives away from the spheres and the cones about the $y_3$ axis that correspond to the points of the partitions and away from the sphere $\sigma=\sigma_{\mathsf g}$. Continuity of the first derivatives across the interfaces makes this piecewise Hessian the weak Hessian. The set $\mathcal A$ contains $(-\iota,-l)$ with $(\iota,l)$, with the complex conjugate data, so that the terms of (B.6) come in conjugate pairs; and it contains $(\iota^\flat,l)$ with $(\iota,l)$, with $\mathsf A(\sigma,-\eta)$ and $-\mathsf B(\sigma,-\eta)$ in place of $\mathsf A(\sigma,\eta)$ and $\mathsf B(\sigma,\eta)$, while $\mathsf S$ and $\mathsf T$ are odd in $\eta$. With these relations the field is invariant under the second pair of (B.1), and it is invariant under the first because its harmonics are those of (B.2). It is therefore $\Gamma$-invariant, since every element of $\Gamma$ is composed of powers of these two pairs and of a translation of $\theta$ by an integer.

 P^2\leq\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}+Q^2,\qquad
 P^2=\tfrac3{50}\,\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2+c_\mu\,\|v\|_\mu^2,\qquad
 Q^2=\tfrac3{50}\,[F]^2+1000\,|\ell(v)|^2,
$$ with $P,Q\geq0$. Cauchy–Schwarz and the multiplier bound give $\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}\leq aP$, where $a=c_{\mathsf M}\|F\|_{\mathcal H}\geq0$, because $\frac3{50}\|v\|_w^2+c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2\leq P^2$. Completing the square in $P^2\leq aP+Q^2$ gives $(P-\frac12a)^2\leq Q^2+\frac14a^2\leq(Q+\frac12a)^2$. Hence $P\leq a+Q$. Using $\sqrt{x+y}\leq\sqrt x+\sqrt y$ for $x,y\geq0$ in the definition of $Q$, we obtain $$

changes.adapted_text: For each resolved harmonic the cell has finitely many unknowns, linear functionals of one mode of a perturbation and of its pressure in the cell: the coefficients of its gradient and of its components in products of orthonormal polynomials of degree at most $\mathsf d$ and $\mathsf d-1$ in each variable, moments of its traces and of the pressure on the sides, and values at corners. To these are added $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, a vector $\zeta\in\mathbb R^n$ and finitely many further unknowns. A trace of the perturbation or its associated pressure can occur in two neighbouring cells, so their local unknowns cannot be chosen independently. We use one real vector $x_{\mathrm g}=(x_{\mathrm p},x_{\mathrm f})$. The perturbation and the given coefficients $\beta$ fix $x_{\mathrm p}$. The free coordinates $x_{\mathrm f}$ include $\zeta$ and will be chosen in the proof of Proposition B.8. The matrix $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}$ reads off the unknowns for cell $\mathsf Q$ from this one vector. The matrices $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}$ are formed by relations that hold for every perturbation, such as the continuity of a trace across a side, the symmetry at the plane $z=0$, or the divergence equation on a side. The vectors of unknowns of a cell are complex, and $\langle\mathsf Ax,x\rangle$ denotes the real part of the form of a matrix $\mathsf A$ on a vector $x$.

changes.adapted_text: We need to choose $x_{\mathrm f}$ so that $(x_{\mathrm p},x_{\mathrm f})$ is orthogonal to every column of every $\mathsf Y_\xi$ while $x_{\mathrm p}$ stays fixed. Write $\mathcal Y^\perp$ for this orthogonal subspace. The zero input tests whether a nonzero vector in $\mathcal Y^\perp$ can have every prescribed coordinate equal to zero. With $v=0$, $\beta=0$ and $F=0$, we have $x_{\mathrm p}=0$, and the right side of (B.44) becomes $-|\zeta|^2/1000$. Thus $\langle\mathsf N x,x\rangle\le0$ on the free-coordinate space $E_{\mathrm f}=\{(0,x_{\mathrm f})\}$. Lemma B.7 makes the same form strictly positive on nonzero vectors in $\mathcal Y^\perp$. The two subspaces therefore intersect only at zero, so the projection $(x_{\mathrm p},x_{\mathrm f})\mapsto x_{\mathrm p}$ is injective on $\mathcal Y^\perp$. In the full space $E$ the column count gives $\operatorname{codim}_E\mathcal Y^\perp\le\dim E_{\mathrm f}$. Thus $\dim\mathcal Y^\perp$ is at least the dimension of the prescribed-coordinate space. The injective projection is consequently onto, or equivalently $E=\mathcal Y^\perp\oplus E_{\mathrm f}$. Returning to $v$, $\beta$ and $F$, we write $(x_{\mathrm p},0)$ as the sum of an element of $\mathcal Y^\perp$ and of a vector $(0,-x_{\mathrm f})$. Then $(x_{\mathrm p},x_{\mathrm f})\in\mathcal Y^\perp$, and $\langle\mathsf N\,x_{\mathrm g},x_{\mathrm g}\rangle\ge0$ for this $x_{\mathrm f}$. $\square$

*Proof.* Let $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. Since $f_*$ vanishes for $|y|\le r_\chi$, the radial phase $f_\alpha(|y|^2)$ coincides in $B_{r_\chi}$ with $f(|y|^2)$, with all its derivatives. The fields $W_\alpha^i$ and the functions $q^i$ depend on the phase only through the factors $E_{\iota,l}$ and the operators $\mathcal V_l$ of (B.5); hence in $\mathbb R\times B_{r_\chi}$ they coincide, with their derivatives, with $W_0^i$ and with the functions $q^i$ for the phase $f$. In the formula for $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ of Subsection B.1 we substitute $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=W_0^0+\sum_i\alpha_iW_0^i$, $q_\alpha=q^0+\sum_i\alpha_iq^i$, $1/S(\alpha)=1/S(0)+\varsigma\cdot\alpha$ and $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)=\beta^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\beta^i$, and we collect the powers of $\alpha$: almost everywhere in $\mathbb R\times B_{r_\chi}$, $$
F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=F^{(0)}+\sum_i\alpha_i\,F^{(i)}+\sum_{i\le i'}\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}\,F^{(ii')}.
$$ The fields (B.57) are bounded on $(0,1)\times B_{r_\chi}$ (Subsection B.1), and $$
\begin{aligned}
V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_j\rangle_{\mathcal H}-d_j\,\alpha_j={}&\bigl[V_j\cdot\beta^0-\langle F^{(0)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi\bigr]+\sum_i\alpha_i\bigl[V_j\cdot\beta^i-\langle F^{(i)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi\bigr]-d_j\,\alpha_j\\
&-\sum_{i\le i'}\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}\,\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi-\bigl\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi},\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal H}.
\end{aligned}
$$ By (B.58) the first bracket is at most $|\mathsf C_j^0|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_j^0$ in absolute value, the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ is at most $|\mathsf C_{ji}^1|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{ji}^1$ for $i\ne j$ and, with the term $-d_j\,\alpha_j$, at most $|\mathsf C_{jj}^1-d_j|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{jj}^1$ for $i=j$, and the coefficient of $\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}$ is at most $|\mathsf C_{jii'}^2|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{jii'}^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the exterior pairing by $\mathsf n_F^{\mathrm{out}}\mathsf n_j^{\mathrm{out}}$. The parameter set (7.29) gives $|\alpha_i|\le\hat\varrho_i$: for $i\in\mathcal J$ this is its coordinate constraint; for $i\notin\mathcal J$, retain the nonnegative summand $d_i^2\alpha_i^2\le\varrho_*^2$ and divide by $|d_i|>0$. The assumptions $d_i\ne0$ and $\varrho_*\ge0$ are those of Subsection 7.3. Substituting these bounds yields $o_j$ in (B.59). With $\bar\ell\equiv0$, the resulting inequality is (7.34). $\square$

Besides the expressions of the coefficients of (B.16) and lower bounds for them, they concern the normalization of the pressure in the cells, under which the matrix of a cell is invariant when a constant is added to its pressure; the rules by which the unknowns of the cells are expressed through the global ones; the parts of $W^{\mathrm r}$ and of its derivatives that the polynomial models leave out, and the groups of harmonics that they couple; the bounds for the errors that are absorbed in each cell; the rectangles near the plane $y_3=0$; and the symmetry of these data under $\iota\mapsto-\iota$. changes.adapted_text: At $s=0$ the computed $\bar W$ concentrates vorticity in a column about the $y_3$ axis and two layers flanking $y_3=0$. Each layer leaves the column in nineteen spiral arms (Figure 1). The axisymmetric angular mean of $\bar W$ has swirl of opposite signs across $y_3=0$, as $R_*$ requires. Its azimuthal vorticity forms a thin layer parallel to the plane that turns along the axis around the column. The mean stream-function contours follow it (Figure 2, left and middle). The $\phi$-dependent part is comparable in size to the mean, with first harmonics $e^{\pm19i\phi}$ largest near the plane at the outer end of the layer (Figure 2, right). A horizontal section shows nineteen vertical-vorticity arms, each ending in a vortex (Figure 3). The angular mean has period $\bar S/2$ in $s$ by half-period symmetry.
changes.authors_text: Figures 1, 2 and 3 show $\bar W$ at $s=0$. Its vorticity is concentrated in a column about the $y_3$ axis and, on either side of the plane $y_3=0$, in a layer that leaves the column and is divided into nineteen spiral arms (Figure 1). The mean of $\bar W$ over the angle $\phi$ is an axisymmetric field with swirl. Its azimuthal component has opposite signs on the two sides of the plane $y_3=0$, as the invariance under $R_*$ requires. Its azimuthal vorticity is concentrated in a thin layer, which runs along the plane at a distance from it and then turns into the direction of the axis, where it encloses the column, and the level lines of its stream function follow this layer (Figure 2, left and middle). The part of $\bar W$ that depends on $\phi$ is of the same order of magnitude as the mean. Its first harmonics, $e^{\pm19i\phi}$, are largest near the plane, about the outer end of the layer (Figure 2, right), and in a horizontal plane through the layer the vertical component of the vorticity forms nineteen spiral arms, which end in nineteen vortices (Figure 3). The mean over $\phi$ has period $\bar S/2$ in $s$, by the symmetry.

All harmonics use one partition in $(\sigma,\eta)$: radial rings, the last extending to infinity, and intervals in $\eta\ge0$. The $R_*$ relations of Subsection B.1 determine $y_3<0$ and impose conditions at $\eta=0$. On each rectangle, a harmonic has its own degrees in $\sigma$ and $\eta$, or is absent. The basis functions satisfy the joining orders in Subsection B.1. This representation is divergence-free, has the axis, origin and far-field behaviour prescribed by the factors in (B.7)–(B.8), and satisfies the symmetries.

authors: C.2 The discretization and Newton’s method#2
changes.note: Separates test equations, numerical integration, the translation condition and the residual diagnostic, preserving the separate certificate residual requirement. Separates the fitted residual used to guide the search from the uniform residual inequalities needed by Section 7.
adapted: C.2 The discretization and Newton’s method#2
changes.adapted_text: We impose (C.1) weakly, integrating over one period and $\mathbb R^3$ against fields on the same partition, of the same form with $h=3$ in place of $h=1$. There are as many test fields as unknown coefficients. The test fields are divergence-free, so the pressure term drops out. We evaluate products in $\operatorname{curl}W\times W$ on a grid in the two harmonic angles and use Gauss quadrature on each rectangle. The unknown period adds a column to the Newton system, and an equation fixing translation in $s$ adds a row. To judge the current iterate, we evaluate the left-hand side of (C.1) without $\nabla H$ on a larger set of harmonics, subtract a gradient fitted by least squares, and measure the remainder in $\mathcal H$ of Subsection 7.1. This gives a numerical approximation to the smallest residual attainable by varying $H$. The certificate requires bounds (7.23) for the specified representative of (7.10), uniformly over its parameter set.
replaced: C.2 The discretization and Newton’s method#2
changes.authors_text: The equation is imposed in a weak form. We integrate (C.1) over a period and over $\mathbb R^3$ against fields of the same form on the same partition, with the exponent $h=3$ in place of $h=1$. These test fields are divergence-free, so that the term $\nabla H$ drops out, and there are as many of them as there are unknown coefficients. The products of harmonics in $\operatorname{curl}W\times W$ are formed on a grid in the two angles on which the harmonics depend, the integrals over each rectangle are computed by Gauss quadrature, and one further equation fixes the translation of the field in $s$; it is the equation that belongs to the unknown period. A computed field is judged by its residual: the left-hand side of (C.1) without $\nabla H$, computed pointwise from the representation on a set of harmonics larger than that of the field, after subtraction of a gradient fitted to it by least squares, and measured in the space $\mathcal H$ of Subsection 7.1. This number approximates the norm in $\mathcal H$ of the left-hand side of (C.1) for the best choice of $H$, and it steers the computation. The bounds (7.23) for the residuals (7.10) of a certificate are among the conditions that the rigorous computation verifies.

changes.note: Splits the continuation narrative into successive operations while preserving its forces, parameter values, wave numbers and two families.
changes.adapted_text:
The starting field for Newton’s method is obtained by continuation, first with finite differences and <!-- source-page: 74 --> then with spectral elements. These discretizations precede that of Subsection C.2. The continuation uses the family $$
\partial_sU+(1-g)\,U+g\,(y\cdot
abla)U+(U\cdot
abla)U+
abla\pi=
u\,\Delta U+F,\qquad\operatorname{div}U=0,
$$ with scaling parameter $g$, viscosity $
u>0$ and force $F$. The first two equations of (1.2) correspond to $g=	frac12$, $
u=1$, $F=0$. We begin with an axisymmetric steady state at $g$ near $0.502$ and with a small force. It is computed from a field with swirl changing sign across $y_3=0$, an inward-flowing layer along that plane, a column, and an axial jet. On the layer we superpose finite-amplitude waves of azimuthal wave numbers $14$ to $20$, turning rigidly about the axis. We reduce the force to zero along with the damping introduced at this step. We then work in $y_3>0$ with one wave family and allow its azimuthal wave number to be real. The unforced states form two-parameter families, with $g$ depending on those parameters. The first family has $g>	frac12$ throughout; a second reaches $g=	frac12$. At that value we superpose a state with its oppositely turning image under $R_*$ and impose the exact condition at $y_3=0$. Further refinements use viscosity in place of $g$ as an unknown and bring the wave number to $19$. We finally project the result onto a space of the form used in Subsection C.2.
changes.authors_text:
Newton’s method starts from a field that was reached by continuation, in other discretizations than that of Subsection C.2: finite differences, and <!-- source-page: 74 --> then spectral elements. The continuation takes place in the family of equations $$
\partial_sU+(1-g)\,U+g\,(y\cdot
abla)U+(U\cdot
abla)U+
abla\pi=
u\,\Delta U+F,\qquad\operatorname{div}U=0,
$$ with a scaling parameter $g$, a viscosity $
u>0$ and a force $F$; the first two equations of (1.2) are the case $g=	frac12$, $
u=1$, $F=0$. It begins with an axisymmetric steady state for $g$ near $0.502$ and a small force, computed from a field whose swirl changes sign across the plane $y_3=0$ and which is composed of a layer of fluid that flows inward along the plane, a column, and a jet along the axis. On this layer we superpose waves of finite amplitude, with azimuthal wave numbers from $14$ to $20$, whose dependence on time is a rigid rotation about the axis, and we bring the force to zero, together with a damping term that this step introduces. We then pass to the half space $y_3>0$, with one family of waves and with the azimuthal wave number as a real parameter. Without force the states so computed form two-parameter families, on which $g$ is a function of the parameters; on the first of these $g>	frac12$ everywhere, and the value $g=	frac12$ is reached on a second one. At $g=	frac12$ we superpose such a state and its image under $R_*$, which turns in the opposite sense, and we replace the condition at the plane $y_3=0$ by the exact one. Finally, through several refinements of the discretization, in which the viscosity takes the place of $g$ as an unknown, the wave number is brought to the integer $19$, and the result is projected onto a space of the form of Subsection C.2.

changes.note: Makes the nine discretizations and the changes in which parameters are unknown easy to follow. Writes out the viscosity change behind the normalization and distinguishes this continuum identity from the finite discretizations. It follows by direct substitution in the displayed continuation equation.
changes.adapted_text:
Starting from this field, we use nine successive discretizations of Subsection C.2, transferring each computed field to the next set of degrees. In the first three, viscosity and period are unknown, and we normalize the mean swirl. For the continuum equations, solutions at different viscosities are dilations of one another; the normalization chooses one. For $g=	frac12$ and $F=0$, the dilation is $U_
u(s,y)=\sqrt
u\,U_1(s,y/\sqrt
u)$, with $\pi_
u(s,y)=
u\pi_1(s,y/\sqrt
u)$ in the continuation equation. We bring the viscosity to one along this family. The fourth discretization fixes it at one and solves for the period. That period is $ ar S$ and is fixed in the last five discretizations. The ninth field is $ ar W$.
changes.authors_text: From this starting field the approximate profile is computed in nine successive discretizations of the form of Subsection C.2, each of which starts from the field of the one before, transferred to the new degrees. In the first three the viscosity is an unknown beside the period, and a normalization of the mean swirl is imposed: for the equations themselves, the solutions for different viscosities are dilations of one another, and the normalization selects one of them. The viscosity is then brought to one along this family. In the fourth discretization the viscosity is one and the period is an unknown; the period found there is $\bar S$, and it is kept in the five discretizations that follow. The ninth field is $\bar W$.

changes.note: Distinguishes the two degree-selection rules and then states the common far-field rule.
changes.adapted_text: Between discretizations we choose degrees separately for each harmonic and rectangle. One rule raises or lowers them using residual size and coefficient decay, adding omitted harmonics wherever they contribute to the residual. The other uses coefficient decay weighted by the estimated local rates of the equation’s terms. Far out, the radial phase removes the spiral oscillation. The remaining frequencies in $\log|y|$ set the radial degrees, and all rings use the same degrees in $\eta$.
changes.authors_text: Between two discretizations the degrees are changed harmonic by harmonic and rectangle by rectangle, by one of two rules. In the first, the contribution of each harmonic on each rectangle to the residual, and the rate at which its coefficients decay with the degree, decide whether its degrees are raised or lowered, and harmonics are added on the rectangles on which the residual lies outside those that are present. In the second, the degrees are predicted from the decay of the coefficients alone, each weighted by estimates of the local rates of the terms of the equation. Far from the origin, where the radial phase has removed the oscillation of the spiral arms, the degrees in the radius are tied to the frequencies in $\log|y|$ that remain, and the degrees in $\eta$ are the same in all rings.

authors: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#1
changes.note: Separates selection of forcing and constraint pairs from their cutoff, spline fit and coefficient rounding, retaining the displayed pairing identity.
adapted: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#1
changes.adapted_text:
We compute $b_i$ and the constraint fields $\Xi_i$ in (7.11) from the equation linearized about one field in the sequence of Subsection C.3. Perturbations are discretized more coarsely than that field. For a given right-hand side, we solve with (C.2), bordered by the period derivative and a condition removing translation in $s$. We measure perturbations in a norm of the form (7.14) with constant weight $w>0$, and right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$. Block Lanczos iteration gives right-hand sides with the largest ratio of solution norm to right-hand-side norm, together with their solutions. We retain finitely many pairs and add the time-translation pair: the left null vector of the bordered system and the field’s $s$-derivative. In each pair, the right-hand side gives $b_i$ and the solution $v_i$ gives the constraint <!-- source-page: 75 --> through $w\,v_i-\Delta v_i$. For a divergence-free field $v$, $$
 igl\langle
abla v,
abla(w\,v_i-\Delta v_i) igrangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\Delta v,\Delta v_iangle_{\mathcal H}+w\,\langle
abla v,
abla v_iangle_{\mathcal H}
$$ is the inner product of $v$ and $v_i$ in this norm. Radial cutoff and smoothing preserve solenoidality and symmetry. For $\Phi_i$ and $\Xi_i$ of Subsection B.1 we repeatedly quarter a meridional cell. Up to normalization, $\Phi_i$ is $r$ times a least-squares spline with coefficients in integer multiples of a power of $2$. The rounded cellwise polynomial $\Xi_i$ approximates $
abla\Phi_i$. Rounding breaks the gradient identity for $\Xi_i$, producing the error $c_\Xi$.
replaced: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#1
changes.authors_text:
The forcing fields $b_i$ and the fields $\Xi_i$ of the constraints (7.11) are computed from the equation linearized about a field of the sequence of Subsection C.3. On a space of perturbations coarser than that of the field, we solve the equation with the operator (C.2) for a given right-hand side, bordered as in Newton’s method by the derivative with respect to the period and by a condition that removes the translation in $s$. Perturbations are measured in a norm of the form of (7.14) with a constant weight $w>0$, and right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$. A block Lanczos iteration gives the right-hand sides for which the solution is largest relative to the right-hand side, with their solutions. Finitely many of these pairs are kept, and to them is added the pair that accounts for the translations in time: the left null vector of the bordered system and the derivative of the field in $s$. For each pair, the forcing field $b_i$ is obtained from the right-hand side, and the constraint from the solution $v_i$, <!-- source-page: 75 --> through the field $w\,v_i-\Delta v_i$: for a divergence-free field $v$, $$
 igl\langle
abla v,
abla(w\,v_i-\Delta v_i) igrangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\Delta v,\Delta v_iangle_{\mathcal H}+w\,\langle
abla v,
abla v_iangle_{\mathcal H}
$$ is the inner product of $v$ and $v_i$ that belongs to this norm. Both fields are cut off in the radius and smoothed, in such a way that they remain divergence-free and keep the symmetries. The fields $\Phi_i$ and $\Xi_i$ of Subsection B.1 are then produced on a mesh of cells of the meridian plane, obtained by repeated division of a cell into four: $\Phi_i$ is, up to a normalization, $r$ times a spline fitted by least squares, whose coefficients are integer multiples of a power of $2$, and $\Xi_i$ is a polynomial on each cell, with rounded coefficients, which approximates $
abla\Phi_i$. This is why $\Xi_i$ is not a gradient, and why Subsection B.1 has the number $c_\Xi$.

changes.adapted_text: The fields $W^i$ in (B.9), $1\le i\le n$, together with $\beta^i$ and $\varsigma_i$, approximately solve the linearized equation with prescribed constraint values. The unknowns include a combination of the forcing fields and a change of period. They solve approximately the equation $F^{(i)}\simeq0$, with $F^{(i)}$ as in (B.57). Here $\simeq$ means equality modulo gradients as defined in (7.2); the numerical approximation concerns satisfaction of that equation. Changing the period changes its associated radial phase. We make this phase change only outside a ball, using $f_*$ in (B.9), so the approximate profiles remain affine in the parameter inside the ball. The adjoint fields $\psi_j$ approximately solve the adjoint linearized equation. As in (7.33), the right-hand sides are combinations of the fields representing the constraints. Their pairings with the forcing fields are prescribed and compared in (7.35) with the columns of $V$. We seek these fields with $h=3$.
replaced: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#2
changes.authors_text: The fields $W^i$ of (B.9), $1\le i\le n$, with the vectors $\beta^i$ and the numbers $\varsigma_i$ of Subsection B.1, are computed approximate solutions of the linearized equation in which a combination of the forcing fields and a change of the period are unknowns and the values of the constraints are prescribed: with the field $F^{(i)}$ of (B.57), they solve approximately the equation $F^{(i)}\simeq0$. A change of the period changes the radial phase, which is tied to the period. In these fields the change is made only outside a ball, which is the origin of the function $f_*$ of (B.9), so that inside the ball the approximate profiles are affine in the parameter. The adjoint fields $\psi_j$ are computed approximate solutions of the adjoint of the linearized equation whose right-hand sides are combinations of the fields that represent the constraints, as (7.33) requires, with prescribed pairings with the forcing fields, which (7.35) compares with the columns of the matrix $V$; they are sought with the exponent $h=3$.

authors: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#3
changes.note: Makes the rotating-frame frequency substitution and the optimization objective explicit without changing either frequency formula or the heuristic for the best weight. Recalls the weight and frequency hypotheses needed for the positive contributions, next to their use. States the nonzero-speed qualification and the elementary optimization underlying the local heuristic, with all other errors omitted as the paper specifies.
adapted: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#3
changes.adapted_text: The multiplier weights $\lambda_p$ and $\mu_p$ in (B.14) act outside $|\iota_2|\le j_*$, $|\iota_2-\iota_1|\le j_*$. We use rotation rates $\nu_p=\pm2\pi/(19\bar S)$, those of the two patterns in Subsection C.1. Substituting these rates in (B.15) gives $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$ in the first rotating frame and $-4\pi(\iota_1-\iota_2)/\bar S$ in the second. Outside the stated range, at least one frequency has modulus greater than $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. The multiplier supplies positive terms proportional to $\lambda_p|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ and $\mu_p|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ in (B.16). This uses the nonnegative weights and the positive-frequency condition on each $\mathcal N_p$ from Subsection B.2; the sign in (B.14) treats $-\mathcal N_p$. These terms must absorb errors including transport by $W^{\mathrm r}+\tfrac12y-\nu_p\,\mathbf e_z\times y$, the velocity relative to that frame. Considering only this error and omitting weight derivatives, the best pointwise weight is proportional to frequency divided by the square of this speed. For positive fixed auxiliary factors and nonzero speed, this follows by maximizing the linear frequency gain minus the quadratic transport error as a function of the weight. The weights are splines in (B.3). Numerical optimization chooses their coefficients to maximize the least, over cells and harmonic classes, of the suitably normalized differences between the two sides of the inequalities containing them.
replaced: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#3
changes.authors_text: The weights $\lambda_p$ and $\mu_p$ of the multiplier (B.14) act on the harmonics outside the range $|\iota_2|\le j_*$, $|\iota_2-\iota_1|\le j_*$. In the computation the rates of rotation $\nu_p$ are, up to the sign, the angular velocity $2\pi/(19\,\bar S)$ of the two patterns of Subsection C.1. In the frame that turns with the first pattern the frequency (B.15) of the harmonic $\iota$ is $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$, and in the frame that turns with the second it is $-4\pi(\iota_1-\iota_2)/\bar S$: outside the range each harmonic has, in one of the two frames, a frequency of modulus larger than $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. The multiplier turns this frequency into positive terms, proportional to $\lambda_p\,|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ and to $\mu_p\,|\Omega_p(\iota)|$, in the coefficients of (B.16). Among the errors that these terms have to absorb is the transport by $W^{\mathrm r}+\tfrac12y-\nu_p\,\mathbf e_z\times y$, the velocity relative to this frame; if this error alone is taken into account, without the derivatives of the weight, the best weight at a point is proportional to the frequency divided by the square of this speed. The weights are splines in the variables (B.3), and their coefficients are found by a numerical optimization, which maximizes the smallest, over the cells and over the classes of harmonics, of the differences between the two sides of the inequalities in which the weights enter, each suitably normalized.
